items.citation: Andrew R. Barron. Universal approximation bounds for superpositions of a sigmoidal function. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 39(3):930-945, 1993. UNVERIFIED: the paper could not be opened; details come from search-result snippets.
items.finding: This is the original Maurey-sampling result for networks. Suppose f has Fourier first moment C_f and B is a ball of radius r. Then for every n there is an n-unit sigmoidal network f_n with integrated squared error over B at most (2rC_f)^2/n. The snippet shows the constant c = (2rC_f)^2. Any linear combination of n fixed basis functions instead has error at least about (1/n)^(2/d). From memory, and not confirmed: the existence proof uses Maurey's probabilistic lemma (draw n atoms i.i.d. from the normalized |Fourier| measure; the variance is at most (2rC_f)^2/n). It also gives Jones's deterministic greedy version, with the same O(1/n) rate.
items.relevance: Every subsampling compressor below is an instance of this template. The variance bound V^2/k is the quantity the project would certify. The greedy variant is the deterministic alternative to random subsampling. When the candidate atoms are restricted to f's own N neurons, each greedy step costs O(N) evaluations.

items.citation: Francis Bach. Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality with Convex Neural Networks. JMLR 18(19):1-53, 2017. arXiv:1412.8690. UNVERIFIED: jmlr.org and arxiv.org could not be opened; abstract text comes from search snippets.
items.finding: Bach studies one-hidden-layer networks with homogeneous activations such as ReLU and threshold units, with infinitely many units and an l1 (variation-norm) penalty on the output weights. The resulting problem is convex. Snippet: solving it 'is only possible if the non-convex subproblem of addition of a new unit can be solved efficiently.' Convex relaxations of that step keep the generalization bounds. But the author 'was not able to find strong enough convex relaxations to obtain provably polynomial-time algorithms,' and leaves open whether tractable algorithms with non-exponential sample complexity exist. From memory, unconfirmed: the add-a-unit step for threshold or ReLU units is NP-hard in general, since it is related to finding the best halfspace, and Maurey gives k-unit approximations at rate gamma_1/sqrt(k).
items.relevance: This is the precise form of the compute obstacle. Searching for a good new neuron over all of R^d is the hard step. Subsampling or greedy selection from f's own neurons removes it: f has already 'solved' the hard subproblem, so the candidate dictionary is finite (N atoms) and each step is polynomial. The cost is that the bound is in terms of the best sub-network of f, not K_eps(f).

items.citation: Jason M. Klusowski, Andrew R. Barron. Approximation by Combinations of ReLU and Squared ReLU Ridge Functions with l1 and l0 Controls. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, Dec 2018. arXiv:1607.07819. UNVERIFIED: details come from search snippets.
items.finding: The paper gives L-infinity and L2 error bounds for m-term ReLU and squared-ReLU networks, with both l1 and l0 (sparsity) controls on the inner and outer weights. For squared ReLU, the L2 error is inversely proportional to the inner-layer l0 sparsity and needs only sublinear outer-layer l0 sparsity. The L-infinity rates improve on the generic c*v_{f,1}*sqrt(d)*m^(-1/2). One fragment suggests about m^(-1/2-1/(d+2)), but the exponent is not confirmed. Companion lower bounds show the constructions are nearly optimal.
items.relevance: Its l0 controls on the inner weights speak to description length. Subsampling neurons is not enough when each neuron has d dense weights, since L(g) is about k(d+1)b bits. Sparsifying each neuron's inner weights as well (the l0 control) is what lowers L(g) further. The L-infinity results matter because the 0-1 disagreement Pr[sign f != sign g] needs uniform or high-probability pointwise closeness, not just L2.

items.citation: Sanjeev Arora, Rong Ge, Behnam Neyshabur, Yi Zhang. Stronger generalization bounds for deep nets via a compression approach. ICML 2018. arXiv:1802.05296. UNVERIFIED: arxiv.org could not be opened; details come from search snippets and the project's existing literature.md.
items.finding: This paper sets up the compression framework. f is (gamma, S)-compressible if some g_A, from a class of about 2^q nets indexed by a data-independent helper string, matches f's outputs within gamma on the training points. Then g_A generalizes with complexity q. The compressor is a random projection of each layer. It is justified by measured noise-stability properties of trained nets: layer cushion, interlayer cushion, activation contraction and interlayer smoothness. On VGG-19/CIFAR-10 the bound is orders of magnitude below norm-based bounds but still vacuous (about 1e5 per a follow-up, as recorded in literature.md). The bound covers only g_A, not f.
items.relevance: This is the canonical compute-efficient compressor with a bound. It shows that random sampling seeded by a public helper string costs no bits. It also shows the margin-to-disagreement step: if |f-g| <= gamma wherever |f| > gamma, then sign f = sign g there. With known D_X, Pr_x[|f(x)| <= gamma] and Pr_x[|f-g| > gamma] are both certifiable by sampling, so Arora's restriction to training points can be dropped.

items.citation: Cenk Baykal, Lucas Liebenwein, Igor Gilitschenski, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. Data-Dependent Coresets for Compressing Neural Networks with Applications to Generalization Bounds. ICLR 2019. arXiv:1804.05345. UNVERIFIED: arxiv.org and openreview.net could not be opened; details come from search snippets.
items.finding: The method importance-samples the weights of a trained fully connected net. Each weight's sampling probability is set by an 'empirical sensitivity', its maximum relative contribution to its output neuron, estimated on a small batch of inputs. Sampled weights are reweighted to stay unbiased. The paper gives instance-dependent and instance-independent bounds on the compressed size as functions of the tolerance eps and the failure probability delta. A corollary is a generalization bound in terms of sensitivity. Per literature.md, pre-activations stay within (1 +/- eps) with high probability over a fresh input. The exact sample-size theorem was not retrieved; from memory it is about S*log(1/delta)/eps^2 per neuron with S the total sensitivity, unconfirmed. Fully connected only.
items.relevance: This is the closest published version of 'subsample the weights of f, then get a bound'. It is weight-level sampling, which is what cuts per-neuron description length. Its guarantee holds with high probability over x ~ D, which is exactly the Pr_x[f != g] the project certifies by sampling under known D_X. Sensitivities can be computed on fresh uniform Boolean samples at no cost.

items.citation: Lucas Liebenwein, Cenk Baykal, Harry Lang, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. Provable Filter Pruning for Efficient Neural Networks. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1911.07412. The follow-up is Baykal et al., SiPPing Neural Networks: Sensitivity-informed Provable Pruning, SIAM J. Math. Data Sci. 2022, arXiv:1910.05422. VERIFIED: the torchprune GitHub README (opened) confirms authors, venues and the method description. Numbers are UNVERIFIED (snippets).
items.finding: Opened README: sensitivity is 'the product of the data and the weight'. A weight's sensitivity is its maximum relative contribution to its output neuron over a small set of inputs, and PFP extends this to filters. Pruning by empirical sensitivity lets one 'provably quantify the trade-off between the error and sparsity'. Snippets: filters are sampled from an importance distribution proportional to sensitivity, with guarantees on the size and performance of the pruned net. A third-party comparison reports 44.04% of ResNet50 parameters pruned on ImageNet at comparable accuracy (unconfirmed). SiPP works 'regardless of whether the original network is fully trained or randomly initialized' (snippet).
items.relevance: This is a maintained, polynomial-time code base for sensitivity sampling of neurons, filters and weights, usable directly as the search step. It is also empirical evidence that trained convnets can be subsampled substantially at small accuracy loss. Caveat: that loss is measured on natural test data, not as disagreement under a known D_X.

items.citation: Ben Mussay, Margarita Osadchy, Vladimir Braverman, Samson Zhou, Dan Feldman. Data-Independent Neural Pruning via Coresets. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1907.04018. VERIFIED: the GitHub repo and its coreset.py were opened and read. Paper claims are UNVERIFIED (snippets).
items.finding: From the code: each hidden neuron i with input weights (w_i, b_i) gets sensitivity s_i = max_j |a_ji| * |sigma(beta * ||(w_i, b_i)||)|. Here a_ji are the outgoing weights and beta bounds the input norm, so no data is used. Neurons are drawn i.i.d. with probability p_i = s_i / sum s. Outgoing weights are rescaled by count_i/(p_i * total_draws), which is exactly Maurey's unbiased importance-sampling estimator. Snippets: 90% compression of LeNet-300-100 on MNIST while improving accuracy. A multiplicative guarantee for all inputs is impossible (their Theorem 6), so the guarantees are additive, for ReLU among others. Aside: in coreset.py the bias of the compressed layer is taken from points[:, 1] rather than points[:, -1], which looks like a bug if the code is reused.
items.relevance: This is a working implementation of path-norm-style neuron subsampling with a guarantee for every bounded input. On {+-1}^n, ||x|| = sqrt(n), so beta is known exactly. The additive-error caveat is why a margin step is needed to convert closeness into 0-1 disagreement. The code is about 90 lines and easy to adapt for the project's neuron-subsampling experiment.

items.citation: Taiji Suzuki, Hiroshi Abe, Tomoaki Nishimura. Compression based bound for non-compressed network: unified generalization error analysis of large compressible deep neural network. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1909.11274. A related paper is Suzuki et al., Spectral Pruning: Compressing Deep Neural Networks via Spectral Analysis and its Generalization Error, IJCAI 2020, pp. 2839-2846, arXiv:1808.08558. UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets and literature.md.
items.finding: The ICLR paper extends compression bounds from the compressed g to the original f, and can give a better rate than the compressed-net bound by improving the bias term. Per literature.md, it controls the population L2 distance between f and g by the local Rademacher complexity of the difference class, under near-low-rank conditions; Bazinet et al. say its constants are not computable. Spectral pruning picks 'the most informative subset of nodes' in each layer using the eigenvalues of the layer's activation covariance. It defines 'degrees of freedom' from that spectrum. Rapid eigenvalue decay gives low degrees of freedom, hence good compressibility, and a generalization bound with a compression-induced bias-variance tradeoff.
items.relevance: Spectral pruning is a polynomial-time 'select a subset of neurons, then refit' method. Selection plus least-squares reconstruction should beat i.i.d. subsampling. Its degrees of freedom are a computable predictor of how many neurons k are needed. The ICLR paper tackles the f-versus-g gap analytically. Under known D_X that gap is simply certified by sampling, which makes the project's route simpler and computable.

items.citation: Ryan Theisen, Jason M. Klusowski, Huan Wang, Nitish Shirish Keskar, Caiming Xiong, Richard Socher. Global Capacity Measures for Deep ReLU Networks via Path Sampling. arXiv:1910.10245, 2019 (venue not confirmed). UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets.
items.finding: The paper samples input-output paths (path sampling) to show that positively homogeneous networks have sparse approximants. This gives bounds in terms of the norm of the product of weights rather than the product of per-layer norms, and includes a multi-class margin bound. A third-party summary, unconfirmed, says the bounds are polynomial in depth, the complexity relates to a Renyi entropy of the path distribution, and on MNIST/CIFAR-10 'networks which generalize well are more compressible via path sampling.'
items.relevance: This is the deep-network extension of Maurey neuron sampling: sample whole paths with probability proportional to the product of weights. It is poly-time, and the number of samples needed is set by a path-norm quantity computable from f. Its empirical claim, if it holds, bears on whether trained nets are close to simple ones in practice: good generalizers compress better under exactly this sampling scheme.

items.citation: Weinan E, Chao Ma, Lei Wu. A Priori Estimates of the Population Risk for Two-layer Neural Networks. Communications in Mathematical Sciences, 2019. arXiv:1810.06397. UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets; theorem forms are from memory.
items.finding: For path-norm-regularized two-layer networks, both approximation and estimation errors 'scale in the same way as the Monte Carlo error rates.' They depend only on the Barron norm of the target, not on the width, and hold when the width is much larger than the sample size. The discrete path norm sum_i |a_i| ||w_i|| is the analogue of the Barron norm. From memory, unconfirmed: there is an m-neuron f_m with ||f - f_m||^2_{L2} <= 3||f||_B^2/m, and the estimation term is about ||f||_B sqrt(log d / n).
items.relevance: This identifies the quantity governing neuron subsampling: k is about (path norm / tolerance)^2. Mean-field-scaled networks (a_i ~ 1/N) have bounded path norm, so k is independent of N. Lazily trained or NTK nets (a_i ~ 1/sqrt N) have path norm about sqrt N, so i.i.d. subsampling gives essentially no compression. This regime question decides whether subsampling can work for a given trained f.

items.citation: Zhengdao Chen, Grant M. Rotskoff, Joan Bruna, Eric Vanden-Eijnden. A Dynamical Central Limit Theorem for Shallow Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2008.09623 (v3 corrects an error in Theorem 3.5). UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets.
items.finding: A Monte Carlo argument shows that a width-m network's fluctuations around its mean-field limit scale as m^(-1/2). The paper shows these fluctuations stay bounded in mean square throughout training, and vanish in the CLT scaling if the mean-field dynamics converge to a measure that fits the data. The bound is dimension-free, an MC resampling error whose variance is governed by the 2-norm of the limiting measure. The authors propose that norm as a regularizer, since it also controls generalization. A related result is Mei, Misiakiewicz, Montanari, COLT 2019 (arXiv:1902.06015, unverified): dimension-free bounds on the distance between finite-N SGD and the mean-field limit.
items.relevance: This is the formal basis for 'a trained mean-field net is compressible by subsampling particles with error O(1/sqrt k)'. Trained neurons behave like i.i.d. draws from a limiting measure rho. A random k-subset of f's N neurons, rescaled, is then itself approximately a k-particle sample from rho, with function-space error O(||rho||/sqrt k), independent of N.

items.citation: Alexander Shevchenko, Marco Mondelli. Landscape Connectivity and Dropout Stability of SGD Solutions for Over-parameterized Neural Networks. ICML 2020, PMLR 119:8773-8784. arXiv:1912.10095. UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets.
items.finding: For SGD-trained mean-field networks, the paper removes neurons and rescales the rest. The loss change 'is independent of the total number of neurons' and 'depends only on how many neurons are left'. The bound is dimension-free for two-layer nets. For multilayer nets, keeping at least M neurons per layer changes the loss by at most about sqrt((d + log M)/M); this comes from a garbled extraction, so the exact form is provisional. As a consequence, SGD solutions are joined by piecewise-linear low-loss paths. The related Kuditipudi et al., NeurIPS 2019 (arXiv:1906.06247, unverified), assumes dropout stability to explain mode connectivity.
items.relevance: This is direct theoretical support for neuron subsampling: a trained wide net is close to its own k-neuron sub-network, with closeness set by k alone. Caveat: this is closeness in training loss (squared or Lipschitz) on the data distribution. Turning it into 0-1 disagreement needs a margin term, which is certifiable by sampling under known D_X. The result holds only in the mean-field (lambda/N) parameterization, not the NTK one.

items.citation: Mao Ye, Chengyue Gong, Lizhen Nie, Denny Zhou, Adam Klivans, Qiang Liu. Good Subnetworks Provably Exist: Pruning via Greedy Forward Selection. ICML 2020, PMLR 119:10820-10830. arXiv:2003.01794. The follow-up is Mao Ye, Lemeng Wu, Qiang Liu, Greedy Optimization Provably Wins the Lottery: Logarithmic Number of Winning Tickets is Enough, NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2010.15969. VERIFIED: the GitHub README (opened) confirms authors, venues and the core claim. The rates are UNVERIFIED (snippets).
items.finding: Opened README: the method starts from an empty network and greedily adds neurons from the large pretrained net. On a sufficiently large pretrained net this provably finds small sub-networks with lower loss than nets trained directly by gradient descent, and the theory also covers random-weight nets. Snippets: for two-layer nets, a size-n sub-network has loss L*_N + O(1/n), where L*_N is the best loss using the full N neurons. A later paper credits it with the first faster O(n^-2) pruning rate, for two-layer nets under sufficient over-parameterization; the paper only conjectures this rate for deep nets. The NeurIPS 2020 follow-up claims discrepancy O(exp(-c n)) between the pruned and original nets under weak assumptions, so O(log(1/eps)) neurons suffice for eps error. It reports ImageNet gains on ResNet and MobileNetV2/V3.
items.relevance: This is the deterministic, polynomial-time alternative to i.i.d. subsampling: Frank-Wolfe or Jones greedy over f's own neurons. Each step costs O(N * #samples). It can beat the Monte Carlo 1/sqrt(k) rate (1/k in squared loss) and is the natural step-2 search after random subsampling. Under known D_X, the greedy objective (distance to f) can be estimated on fresh uniform samples, with final certification on further fresh samples.

items.citation: Daniel Hsu, Ziwei Ji, Matus Telgarsky, Lan Wang. Generalization bounds via distillation. ICLR 2021. arXiv:2104.05641. UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets and literature.md.
items.finding: A complex network f inherits the bound of a simpler distilled network g, plus a distillation distance between f and g. That distance is estimated on extra samples from a data-augmentation distribution with bounded density ratio to D_X. The paper also gives a looser classical uniform-convergence analysis of compression. Experiments are on CIFAR-10 and MNIST. Per literature.md, Figure 1 shows standard bounds of about 1e15 shrunk by about 1e10 via distillation (ResNet8), so the bounds still appear well above 1.
items.relevance: This is the published version of the project's reduction err(f) <= bound(g) + Pr[f != g]. With known D_X, as for uniform Boolean inputs, the augmentation distribution is just D_X, with density ratio 1, so the distillation-distance term is cheap and tight. What remains is the search for g, where subsampling or greedy selection from f replaces their gradient-trained distillation.

items.citation: Melih Barsbey, Milad Sefidgaran, Murat A. Erdogdu, Gael Richard, Umut Simsekli. Heavy Tails in SGD and Compressibility of Overparametrized Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2021. arXiv:2106.03614. UNVERIFIED: details come from snippets; the arXiv ID is from memory.
items.finding: The paper proves that networks whose SGD dynamics show (i) mean-field propagation of chaos (neurons become asymptotically independent as width grows) and (ii) heavy-tailed stationary distributions (large step-size/batch-size ratio) are 'p-compressible', with pruning error shrinking as width grows. Experiments on fully connected and convolutional nets confirm that large step/batch ratios induce heavy tails which, together with over-parameterization, give compressibility. Per literature.md, it also has an asymptotic, non-computable 'generalization bound for the uncompressed network'.
items.relevance: This addresses whether trained nets are in practice close to simple functions, and when. Compressibility under magnitude pruning is predicted to depend on the training hyperparameters (step/batch ratio) and on the mean-field regime. This suggests the project should train its Boolean nets in mean-field parameterization, possibly with large learning rates, if it wants subsampling to find short g.

report.synthesis:
Access limits. From this session only github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com were reachable. arxiv.org, openreview.net, jmlr.org, proceedings.mlr.press, Semantic Scholar and the other paper hosts all failed to resolve, so no arXiv abstract page could be opened. Three items count as verified, each from a GitHub page I opened: torchprune for PFP/SiPP, the Mussay coreset code, and the Ye et al. README. Everything else comes from search snippets, from the project's own literature.md, or from memory (flagged as such). Allowing arxiv.org in the session's network settings would let the theorem statements be checked.

What the literature says about the compute question:

1. **Subsampling turns an exponential search into a polynomial one, for a weaker target.** The general step "find a good new unit" is hard. Bach (2017) leaves the existence of a poly-time algorithm open, and from memory it is NP-hard for threshold and ReLU units. Restricting candidates to f's own N neurons removes the hardness, because f has already solved the hard subproblems. Every method here runs in polynomial time:
   * Maurey/Barron i.i.d. sampling: Mussay's code is exactly this.
   * Sensitivity sampling: Baykal, Liebenwein.
   * Path sampling: Theisen.
   * Greedy forward selection: Ye et al.
   * Node selection with refitting: Suzuki's spectral pruning.

   The cost is that the bound is in terms of the shortest sub-network of f, not K_eps(f).

2. **Concrete certified scheme for uniform Boolean inputs** (my derivation from the template above, not quoted from any paper):
   * **Setup.** Take f = sum_i a_i sigma(w_i.x + b_i). Set s_i = sup_x |sigma(w_i.x + b_i)|, which on {+-1}^n is at most ||w_i||_1 + |b_i| for ReLU. Let V = sum_i |a_i| s_i.
   * **Sampling.** Draw k neurons i.i.d. with p_i = |a_i| s_i / V and form g = (V/k) sum_t sign(a_{i_t}) sigma_{i_t} / s_{i_t}.
   * **Pointwise error.** By Hoeffding, for each x, Pr_sample[|f(x) - g(x)| > gamma] <= 2exp(-k gamma^2 / (2V^2)).
   * **Disagreement.** Hence E_sample Pr_x[sign f != sign g] <= Pr_x[|f(x)| <= gamma] + 2exp(-k gamma^2 / (2V^2)). Both terms can be certified on fresh uniform samples.
   * **Neurons needed.** k is about 2(V/gamma)^2 ln(2/eta).
   * **Description length.** A sampled neuron's index into f is not free, because f depends on the data. So L(g) is about k(n+1)b bits, plus one scale. Two refinements lower it: sparsify and quantize each neuron's weights (Baykal/SiPP, Klusowski-Barron l0 controls), or code neurons against a public seeded initialization (Arora's helper string).
   * **Selection is free.** The Occam term is uniform over g, so trying many candidate g's and keeping the best costs nothing there. The disagreement term only needs fresh samples after selection.
   * **Greedy refinement.** Greedy or Frank-Wolfe selection from f's neurons, with least-squares refitting of the output weights, should do better than the Monte Carlo rate. Ye et al. claim O(1/n) in loss generally, O(n^-2) under over-parameterization, and O(exp(-cn)) in the NeurIPS follow-up.

3. **When subsampling works.** The governing quantity is the path or variation norm V relative to the margin gamma.
   * In the mean-field parameterization (a_i ~ 1/N), V stays bounded. Trained neurons behave like i.i.d. particles from a limiting measure (Chen-Rotskoff-Bruna-Vanden-Eijnden; Mei-Misiakiewicz-Montanari). A random k-subset is then within O(1/sqrt k) in L2, independent of N. Shevchenko-Mondelli prove that the loss change after keeping k neurons depends only on k.
   * In the NTK or lazy parameterization (a_i ~ 1/sqrt N), V grows like sqrt N, and i.i.d. subsampling gives essentially no compression.
   * So the project should train its Boolean nets in mean-field scaling. Barsbey et al. add that large step/batch ratios, through heavy tails, increase compressibility.

4. **Are trained nets close to simple functions in practice?** The evidence is supportive but indirect:
   * Mussay: 90% of LeNet-300-100 neurons removed on MNIST with accuracy improved.
   * PFP: about 44% of ResNet50 parameters pruned on ImageNet (third-party figure).
   * Theisen: well-generalizing nets are more compressible by path sampling (third-party summary).
   * The project's literature.md records non-vacuous compression bounds, such as Lotfi 2022.

   All of these measure accuracy on natural test data, not disagreement with f under D_X. For uniform Boolean inputs the two coincide, which is a point in the project's favour.

5. **Gaps.** I found no paper that combines neuron or weight subsampling with a sampling-certified Pr_D[f != g] term under known D_X to bound the original f. Hsu et al. (2021) is the closest. They use gradient-trained distillation with augmentation, and their bounds are still large. The obvious experiment is to compare, on a Boolean task:
   * i.i.d. Maurey subsampling,
   * sensitivity sampling plus weight sparsification,
   * greedy forward selection with refitting,

   each against the oracle K_eps.

Two pointers I could not verify in this sweep. Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky (NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1706.08498) use the Maurey sparsification lemma inside their margin covering bound. Kushilevitz-Mansour/Goldreich-Levin (from memory) use query access to f to find the heavy Fourier coefficients under the uniform distribution in poly(n, 1/theta) time. That is a separate efficient search route that applies whenever f is close to a sparse Fourier polynomial.

Aside: the public Mussay coreset.py sets the compressed layer's bias from points[:, 1] instead of points[:, -1], which looks like a bug if that code is reused.

checks.citation: Andrew R. Barron. Universal approximation bounds for superpositions of a sigmoidal function. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 39(3):930-945, 1993. DOI 10.1109/18.256500.
checks.corrected_finding: The paper exists and the venue, volume, pages and DOI are as stated. I checked it through search results, which included OCR snippets of the paper and abstract. I could not open the full text: doi.org, documents.epfl.ch and stat.yale.edu are not reachable from this session, and arxiv.org would have to be allowed in the session's network settings. Confirmed: (1) Proposition/Theorem 1. For f with finite C_f (the first absolute moment of its Fourier magnitude distribution), every n >= 1 and any probability measure on a ball of radius r, some n-node sigmoidal combination f_n has integrated squared error <= (2rC_f)^2/n. The outer coefficients can be restricted to l1 norm <= 2rC_f. (2) The abstract says fixed-basis expansions with n terms cannot do better than order (1/n)^{2/d} uniformly over the same class. (3) Secondary sources confirm the lineage: Maurey's probabilistic lemma, published by Pisier in 1981, and Jones's 1992 constructive iterative version with the same O(1/n) rate. A 2020 paper cites 'Bar93, Theorem 1 and Lemma 1' for the Maurey-Barron-Jones convex-hull lemma (error c/n for c > b^2 - ||f||^2, where b bounds the atoms). This supports the agent's from-memory description of the proof, but I did not read the proof itself.

checks.citation: Francis Bach. Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality with Convex Neural Networks. JMLR 18(19):1-53, 2017. arXiv:1412.8690.
checks.corrected_finding: The paper, venue and arXiv ID are confirmed by search: jmlr.org/papers/v18/14-546.html and arxiv.org/html/1412.8690. I could not open either page here, because arxiv.org and jmlr.org are blocked in this session. The quoted abstract statements are confirmed. Solving the infinite-width problem requires solving the non-convex add-a-unit subproblem. Convex relaxations keep the generalization bounds. The author 'was not able to find strong enough convex relaxations to obtain provably polynomial-time algorithms', and leaves open whether tractable algorithms with non-exponential sample complexity exist. Correcting the from-memory part: Frank-Wolfe (conditional gradient) in function space gives squared error O(gamma_1^2/k) with k units, i.e. L2 error about gamma_1/sqrt(k), or n = O(gamma_1^2 eps^-2) units for error eps. That part is confirmed. NP-hardness is attributed only to the threshold-unit (alpha = 0) incremental step, via hardness of learning halfspaces with noise (Guruswami-Raghavendra). Bach's own summary describes the ReLU step as having polynomial but potentially high complexity, not as NP-hard. So 'NP-hard for threshold or ReLU' overstates the ReLU case.

checks.citation: Jason M. Klusowski, Andrew R. Barron. Approximation by Combinations of ReLU and Squared ReLU Ridge Functions with l1 and l0 Controls. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 64(12):7649ff, Dec 2018. arXiv:1607.07819 (v1 was titled 'Uniform approximation by neural networks activated by first and second order ridge splines').
checks.corrected_finding: The paper, authors and venue are confirmed (IEEE TIT vol. 64, no. 12, Dec 2018, starting p. 7649). These abstract claims are confirmed: L-infinity and L2 bounds with l1 and l0 controls on inner and outer parameters. For squared ReLU, the L2 error is inversely proportional to the inner-layer l0 sparsity and 'need only be sublinear in the outer layer l0 sparsity'. Companion lower bounds show near-optimality. The abstract also says the constructions use a variant of the Jones-Barron probabilistic method, read as stratified sampling with proportionate allocation or as two-stage cluster sampling. That is directly a subsampling scheme. Correction to the rate: the ReLU L-infinity bound is about c * v_{f,2} * sqrt(d + log m) * m^(-1/2-1/d), from a garbled theorem extraction. The paper says this raises the exponent from 1/2 to 1/2 + O(1/d) over earlier hinging-hyperplane (ReLU) results. The fragment 'm^(-1/2-1/(d+2))' is not supported. The baseline 'c*v_{f,1}*sqrt(d)*m^(-1/2)' was not confirmed; the relevant spectral quantities are v_{f,2} for ReLU and v_{f,3} for squared ReLU.

checks.citation: Sanjeev Arora, Rong Ge, Behnam Neyshabur, Yi Zhang. Stronger generalization bounds for deep nets via a compression approach. ICML 2018. arXiv:1802.05296.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed through search results (ICML 2018 poster page, arXiv 1802.05296, ar5iv). arxiv.org could not be opened directly. Confirmed details: the compression analysis relies on newly identified, experimentally verified 'noise stability' properties of trained nets, namely layer cushion, interlayer cushion, activation contraction and interlayer smoothness. Individual layers are compressed by a linear-algebraic random-projection procedure. The '~1e5' VGG-19/CIFAR-10 figure comes from Li, Sun, Su, Suzuki and Huang (AISTATS 2020, arXiv:2001.05070), which itself notes that the comparison is not direct (CP-VGG-16 vs VGG-19). The bound covers the compressed net only. One caveat: 'Compression Implies Generalization' (arXiv:2106.07989) defines the cushions as reciprocals of Arora's, so check conventions before comparing numbers.

checks.citation: Cenk Baykal, Lucas Liebenwein, Igor Gilitschenski, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. Data-Dependent Coresets for Compressing Neural Networks with Applications to Generalization Bounds. ICLR 2019. arXiv:1804.05345.
checks.corrected_finding: Authors, venue (ICLR 2019) and arXiv ID are confirmed by search: the ICLR poster page, arXiv 1804.05345v3 and the Haifa CRIS record. arxiv.org and openreview.net are blocked here. The abstract confirms an 'empirical notion of sensitivity' that extends coreset constructions to compress the parameters of trained fully connected nets. The output is provably approximated, with instance-dependent and instance-independent bounds on compressed size as functions of the user-specified tolerance and failure probability, and with novel generalization bounds. The method importance-samples parameters. The sensitivity definition (maximum relative contribution of a weight to its output neuron over a small input batch) is confirmed by the companion SiPP/PFP READMEs, which I opened. Not confirmed: the exact sample-size theorem (the from-memory 'S*log(1/delta)/eps^2 per neuron') and the '(1 +/- eps) pre-activation w.h.p. over a fresh input' statement, which comes from literature.md.

checks.citation: Lucas Liebenwein, Cenk Baykal, Harry Lang, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. Provable Filter Pruning for Efficient Neural Networks. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1911.07412. Follow-up: Cenk Baykal, Lucas Liebenwein, Igor Gilitschenski, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. Sensitivity-Informed Provable Pruning of Neural Networks. SIAM J. Math. Data Sci. 4(1):26-45, 2022, DOI 10.1137/20M1383239. The arXiv version is 'SiPPing Neural Networks...', arXiv:1910.05422.
checks.corrected_finding: I opened the READMEs via raw.githubusercontent.com. The quoted phrases are not in the top-level torchprune README. They are in paper/pfp/README.md ('relies on a notion of sensitivity (the product of the data and the weight) to provably quantify the error introduced by pruning'; '...enables us to provably quantify the trade-off between the error and sparsity of the resulting pruned neural network'). paper/sipp/README.md defines weight sensitivity as 'the maximum relative contribution of the weight to the corresponding output neuron over a small set of points'. The journal version of SiPP is titled 'Sensitivity-Informed Provable Pruning of Neural Networks', SIAM J. Math. Data Sci. 4(1):26-45, 2022. Its abstract says the method works 'regardless of whether the original network is fully trained or randomly initialized'. The 44.04% figure is the PFP paper's own result, from its ResNet50/ImageNet table and reproduced by arXiv:2209.08554. In the 'within 1.0% top-1' setting, top-1 error goes from 23.87% to 24.79% (+0.92), with 44.04% of parameters pruned and 30.05% fewer FLOPs. PFP builds its sampling distribution over filters from a small batch of inputs. The ICLR poster lists the authors in a different order from arXiv.

checks.citation: Ben Mussay, Margarita Osadchy, Vladimir Braverman, Samson Zhou, Dan Feldman. Data-Independent Neural Pruning via Coresets. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1907.04018 (OpenReview H1gmHaEKwB).
checks.corrected_finding: I read coreset.py myself. The repo holds only LICENSE, README.md and coreset.py (89 lines), and the README holds only the BibTeX (ICLR 2020). Code details confirmed: sensitivity s_i = max_j|a_ji| * |sigma(beta * ||(w_i,b_i)||)|, normalized to p_i. Neurons are drawn i.i.d. from p, and the outgoing weights are rescaled by count_i/(p_i * cnt). The bias bug is real: the bias is stored as the last column of points, but the code returns points[:, 1] as the new bias. Two more details. First, the loop draws until it has coreset_size distinct neurons, so the total draw count cnt is random rather than fixed, and the estimator is only approximately Maurey's fixed-k unbiased one. Second, the 'Uniform' branch indexes 4-D conv tensors, inconsistent with the FC path. Because the bias coordinate is appended, the norm on {+-1}^n is ||(x,1)|| = sqrt(n+1), not sqrt(n). Paper claims confirmed via search: the abstract says '90% compression of the LeNet-300-100 architecture on MNIST while improving the accuracy' (about 267K to 26K parameters, error 2.16% to 2.03%). Theorem 6 shows small coresets with a multiplicative guarantee cannot exist for ReLU and similar activations, which motivates additive eps-error that holds for any input in the ball.

checks.citation: Taiji Suzuki, Hiroshi Abe, Tomoaki Nishimura. Compression based bound for non-compressed network: unified generalization error analysis of large compressible deep neural network. ICLR 2020. arXiv:1909.11274. Related: Taiji Suzuki, Hiroshi Abe, Tomoya Murata, Shingo Horiuchi, Kotaro Ito, Tokuma Wachi, So Hirai, Masatoshi Yukishima, Tomoaki Nishimura. Spectral Pruning: Compressing Deep Neural Networks via Spectral Analysis and its Generalization Error. IJCAI 2020, pp. 2839-2846, arXiv:1808.08558.
checks.corrected_finding: Both papers are confirmed via search: the ICLR poster ByeGzlrKwH, and IJCAI proceedings 2020/393 with DOI 10.24963/ijcai.2020/393. The ICLR abstract converts compressed-net bounds into bounds for the uncompressed network, with a better rate than the compressed-net bound thanks to an improved bias term. It also gives a data-dependent bound, and its analysis rests on the implicit-bias hypothesis and near-low-rank models. The spectral-pruning abstract defines 'degrees of freedom' from the eigenvalue spectrum of the covariance of internal nodes. It keeps 'the most informative subset of nodes', relates the method to random-feature techniques, and gives a generalization bound with a compression-induced bias-variance tradeoff; rapid eigenvalue decay means low degrees of freedom. The local-Rademacher and non-computable-constants statements come from literature.md and were not rechecked. The full IJCAI author list has nine authors.

checks.citation: Ryan Theisen, Jason M. Klusowski, Huan Wang, Nitish Shirish Keskar, Caiming Xiong, Richard Socher. Global Capacity Measures for Deep ReLU Networks via Path Sampling. arXiv:1910.10245, Oct 2019 (arXiv preprint; no peer-reviewed venue found).
checks.corrected_finding: The paper and authors are confirmed via search: arXiv 1910.10245v1, submitted 22 Oct 2019, stat.ML/cs.LG. No conference or journal version turned up. The abstract says that positively homogeneous networks admit bounds in terms of the norm of the product of weights rather than the product of per-layer norms. The proof extends a sampling argument (Barron and Klusowski 2018) that writes the net as a path distribution and samples from it, giving sparse approximants in a small representer set. That yields covering-number bounds and multi-class generalization bounds that are 'comparable to, and in certain cases improve upon' existing ones. A lower bound shows the sampling analysis is nearly tight, and experiments find that compressibility under path sampling 'correlates well with generalization'. A 1/2-Renyi entropy of the marginal path distributions appears in the analysis. The counting bound 8^{ML}(de)^M gives log-cardinality M(log(de) + L log 8), linear in depth L, which supports 'polynomial in depth'. The specific MNIST/CIFAR-10 random-label details come only from a secondary summary.

checks.citation: Weinan E, Chao Ma, Lei Wu. A Priori Estimates of the Population Risk for Two-layer Neural Networks. Communications in Mathematical Sciences 17(5):1407-1425, 2019. arXiv:1810.06397.
checks.corrected_finding: The venue is confirmed: CMS 17(5), pp. 1407-1425, 2019, DOI 10.4310/CMS.2019.v17.n5.a11. The abstract is confirmed: the estimates are 'nearly optimal in the sense that the error rates scale in the same way as the Monte Carlo error rates', they hold when network size is much larger than the dataset, and they are a priori, depending only on norms of the target and not on model parameters. Correction: the paper's path norm is ||theta||_P = sum_k |a_k| * ||w_k||_1, with the l1 norm of inner weights paired with l_inf-bounded inputs, not ||w_i||_2. The target norm is a spectral/Barron-type gamma_2 norm (keyword 'Barron space'). The from-memory constants (an m-neuron f_m with ||f - f_m||^2 <= 3||f||^2/m, and an estimation term of about ||f|| sqrt(log d / n)) were not confirmed. The 3 lambda ||theta||_P sqrt(2 log(2d)/n) penalty I found is from the companion residual-network paper (arXiv:1903.02154), not this one. The statement that NTK-scaled nets have path norm about sqrt(N) is the agent's own inference and is not in this paper.

checks.citation: Zhengdao Chen, Grant M. Rotskoff, Joan Bruna, Eric Vanden-Eijnden. A Dynamical Central Limit Theorem for Shallow Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2020 (NeurIPS 33). arXiv:2008.09623 (v3, revised Mar 2022, corrects an error in Theorem 3.5). Related: Song Mei, Theodor Misiakiewicz, Andrea Montanari. Mean-field theory of two-layers neural networks: dimension-free bounds and kernel limit. COLT 2019, PMLR 99:2388-2464, arXiv:1902.06015.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed via the NeurIPS proceedings abstract and the arXiv v3 listing. Starting from random initialization, the finite-width network deviates from its mean-field limit at the CLT scale. A dynamical CLT shows these fluctuations stay bounded in mean square during training, controlled by a Monte Carlo resampling error and the 2-norm of the underlying measure, which also governs generalization. That motivates the 2-norm as a regularizer. If the mean-field dynamics converge to a measure that interpolates the data, the deviation eventually vanishes at the CLT scaling. The v3 note 'an error in Theorem 3.5 has been corrected' is confirmed. Mei et al. is confirmed as COLT 2019, PMLR 99:2388-2464: the mean-field description is accurate once width is large relative to input dimension, kernel ridge regression is a special limit, and the analysis covers unbounded activations and noisy SGD. The claim that a random k-subset of f's neurons is approximately a k-particle sample from rho is the agent's own inference, not a result of either paper.

checks.citation: Alexander Shevchenko, Marco Mondelli. Landscape Connectivity and Dropout Stability of SGD Solutions for Over-parameterized Neural Networks. ICML 2020, PMLR 119:8773-8784. arXiv:1912.10095.
checks.corrected_finding: Venue and pages are confirmed. The abstract says the loss change from removing neurons and rescaling the rest 'is independent of the total number of neurons, and it depends only on how many neurons are left'. SGD solutions are connected by piecewise-linear paths whose loss increase vanishes as width grows, and the results are dimension-free for two-layer nets but need width linear in d for multilayer nets. On the exact form, the arXiv appendix snippet supports the agent's provisional formula. Two-layer: loss change of order sqrt(log M / M), independent of N and d. Multilayer, keeping at least M neurons per layer: at most about sqrt((d + log M)/M). The connectivity-path bound scales like sqrt((d + log N)/N). Constants and theorem numbers were not checked. Kuditipudi, Wang, Lee, Zhang, Li, Hu, Ge, Arora, 'Explaining Landscape Connectivity of Low-cost Solutions for Multilayer Nets' (NeurIPS 2019, arXiv:1906.06247) is confirmed: it assumes dropout stability or noise stability and builds piecewise-linear paths (10 segments under noise stability).

checks.citation: Mao Ye, Chengyue Gong, Lizhen Nie, Denny Zhou, Adam Klivans, Qiang Liu. Good Subnetworks Provably Exist: Pruning via Greedy Forward Selection. ICML 2020, PMLR 119:10820-10830. arXiv:2003.01794. Follow-up: Mao Ye, Lemeng Wu, Qiang Liu. Greedy Optimization Provably Wins the Lottery: Logarithmic Number of Winning Tickets is Enough. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2010.15969.
checks.corrected_finding: README (opened): the repo is titled 'Learning Winning Subnetworks via Greedy Optimization', and the README misspells the ICML title as 'Exists'. It describes starting from an empty network and greedily adding important neurons from a large network. On sufficiently large pre-trained nets this 'guarantees to find small subnetworks with lower loss than networks directly trained with gradient descent', it also covers random-weight nets, and it advises fine-tuning rather than re-initializing. Corrections on the rates, from the arXiv text via search: L[f_n] = O(1/n) + L*_N, where L*_N is 'the best possible loss achievable by convex combinations of all the N neurons', not simply the full net's loss. The faster O(1/n^2) rate is in the paper's own contribution list, so it is not merely credited by a later paper. It holds when the large net is sufficiently over-parameterized and can fit the training data under small perturbations, and secondary sources say the proof covers two-layer nets only. I could not confirm that the paper 'conjectures' it for deep nets. NeurIPS 2020 follow-up (proceedings abstract): under weak assumptions the pruned-to-full discrepancy decays exponentially in the pruned size, hence a logarithmic number of neurons suffices, with ImageNet gains on ResNet and MobileNetV2/V3.

checks.citation: Daniel Hsu, Ziwei Ji, Matus Telgarsky, Lan Wang. Generalization bounds via distillation. ICLR 2021. arXiv:2104.05641.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed via the ICLR 2021 poster/spotlight pages and arXiv. Per the abstract, a high-complexity net that distills to a low-complexity net with nearly identical predictions 'inherits' the distilled net's bound, 'assuming the use of well-behaved data augmentation'. The paper also gives a looser classical uniform-convergence analysis of compression, plus CIFAR-10 and MNIST experiments. The Figure 1 numbers are confirmed from the paper text: a standard ResNet with test error 0.008 (MNIST) and 0.067 (CIFAR-10), an observed generalization gap of about 1e-1, standard bounds of about 1e15, and distillation shrinking the bounds by about 1e10. Not confirmed: the 'ResNet8' label, and the precise 'bounded density ratio to D_X' form of the augmentation assumption. The abstract says only 'well-behaved data augmentation'; the density-ratio form comes from literature.md.

checks.citation: Melih Barsbey, Milad Sefidgaran, Murat A. Erdogdu, Gael Richard, Umut Simsekli. Heavy Tails in SGD and Compressibility of Overparametrized Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2021. arXiv:2106.03795 (not 2106.03614).
checks.corrected_finding: The arXiv ID is wrong: the paper is arXiv:2106.03795 (submitted 7 June 2021; NeurIPS 2021 poster 26594), which matches the project's literature.md. Abstract, confirmed via search: as width grows, SGD training approaches a mean-field limit in which weights act independently (propagation of chaos), and a large step-size/batch-size ratio gives a heavy-tailed stationary distribution. Under these two properties the networks are provably 'l_p-compressible' (not 'p-compressible'). The compression errors of magnitude, singular-value and node pruning become arbitrarily small as network size increases. Experiments on FC and conv nets support the claim that large step/batch ratios induce heavy tails, which together with over-parameterization give compressibility. The paper also proves generalization bounds consistent with lower error for more compressible nets. The 'asymptotic, non-computable bound for the uncompressed network' comes from literature.md and was not rechecked. Related follow-up: Wan, Barsbey, Zaidi, Simsekli, ICML 2024, arXiv:2306.08125.

items.citation: Samuel Stanton, Pavel Izmailov, Polina Kirichenko, Alexander A. Alemi, Andrew Gordon Wilson. 'Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?' NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv 2106.05945). UNVERIFIED: page not opened (arxiv.org and proceedings.neurips.cc are blocked in this session). Details below come from search-result snippets of the paper, poster and abstract.
items.finding: The paper separates fidelity (student-teacher agreement) from student generalization. It finds 'a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher', and names optimization difficulty as a key cause. Points from the snippets: (i) on CIFAR-100, with a ResNet-56 student and a 3-member ResNet-56 ensemble teacher, top-1 test agreement stays below about 80-86% even on the largest distillation sets; the poster says the best policy reaches only about 85%. (ii) The student does not even agree with the teacher on the distillation (training) data, so the gap is not a generalization gap. (iii) Adding GAN-generated or augmented distillation data raises test agreement but lowers agreement on the distillation set. (iv) Longer training and other optimizers change little. (v) In the ResNet-20 self-distillation experiment on CIFAR-100, the student is initialized at a mix lambda*theta_teacher + (1-lambda)*random. For lambda <= 0.25 it converges to a sub-optimal distillation loss and disagrees substantially with the teacher; at lambda = 0.375 the loss reaches its optimum and agreement 'drastically increases'. One snippet also says a student distilled from a single teacher can exceed 99% test agreement with enough data; I could not confirm which setting that refers to.
items.relevance: This is the main evidence that finding a g close to f is limited by optimization, not capacity. In self-distillation g = f exists in the search space, yet SGD from a random start does not find it. For our bound, gradient-based distillation from scratch can leave Pr[f != g] at about 15% on hard tasks, which wipes out the gain. The lambda result points to starting g near f's own weights, as subsampling or pruning f does. It also shows that unlimited fresh inputs (our known-D_X case) do not on their own remove the optimization gap.

items.citation: Yiding Jiang, Vaishnavh Nagarajan, Christina Baek, J. Zico Kolter. 'Assessing Generalization of SGD via Disagreement.' ICLR 2022 (spotlight), arXiv 2106.13799. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from search snippets and the ICLR page.
items.finding: If you train the same architecture on the same data twice with different SGD randomness, the two networks disagree on unlabeled test inputs at a rate close to the test error. This is the 'Generalization Disagreement Equality'. It nearly holds for ResNets, CNNs and fully connected networks on CIFAR-10/100 and SVHN, including runs that differ only in seed. The deviation is slightly larger when only initialization or data order varies. The authors prove that GDE follows from calibration of the ensemble. A TMLR note by Kirsch and Gal reports that calibration gets worse under distribution shift.
items.relevance: This gives a baseline for how close a g must be. An independently trained g, even one with the same architecture, sits at Pr[f != g] of about err(f), so the bound becomes about 2*err(f) plus the Occam term. A g that helps must be fitted to f specifically (distillation, or subsampling f's weights), and must beat this run-to-run disagreement. Any 'close to a simple function' claim should be measured against it.

items.citation: Sara Hooker, Aaron Courville, Gregory Clark, Yann Dauphin, Andrea Frome. 'What Do Compressed Deep Neural Networks Forget?' arXiv 1911.05248 (2019; an earlier version was an ICLR 2020 submission on OpenReview). UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets.
items.finding: Pruned and dense models have similar top-line accuracy but differ on a small subset of inputs, the 'Pruning Identified Exemplars' (PIEs). Sparsity affects PIEs systematically. They are disproportionately atypical, noisy, mislabeled, low-quality or fine-grained images, and removing them from the test set greatly improves top-1 accuracy for both sparse and dense models. A ResNet-50 on ImageNet can have 90% of its weights removed by magnitude pruning for a top-1 loss of under 3 points absolute. On CIFAR-10, PIEs are identified with 30 dense and 30 sparse wide ResNets. I could not retrieve the exact PIE counts or the modal-label criterion.
items.relevance: Compressing f by pruning keeps g close to f in function space. The disagreement concentrates on a small, identifiable set of hard inputs instead of being spread out. At 90% sparsity Pr[f != g] >= |acc(f) - acc(g)|, which is about 3% on ImageNet; the paper reports set-level differences, not pointwise agreement. Pruning starts from f's weights, so it supports a 'subsample f, then fine-tune' approach over distilling from scratch.

items.citation: Utku Evci, Yani Ioannou, Cem Keskin, Yann Dauphin. 'Gradient Flow in Sparse Neural Networks and How Lottery Tickets Win.' AAAI 2022 (vol. 36, pp. 6577-6586), arXiv 2010.03533. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets and a secondary summary.
items.finding: Lottery tickets do not improve gradient flow. They succeed by re-learning the pruning solution they came from: their initializations are closer to the pruning solution, and trained tickets end up in the same basin of attraction, which explains their functional similarity to that solution. Sparse networks trained from a random sparse initialization have poor gradient flow and do worse. The basin and functional-similarity wording comes from a secondary summary.
items.relevance: This is more evidence that a small network matching f is easy to reach only from near f's own parameters and hard to reach from scratch. The same initialization effect appears in Stanton et al. A subsample-of-f initialization is the natural way to make the search for g polynomial.

items.citation: Lucas Liebenwein, Cenk Baykal, Brandon Carter, David Gifford, Daniela Rus. 'Lost in Pruning: The Effects of Pruning Neural Networks beyond Test Accuracy.' MLSys 2021, arXiv 2103.03014. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets of the abstract and introduction.
items.finding: The paper introduces classification-based functional distance metrics between a pruned network and its parent. Pruned models stay functionally similar enough to the uncompressed parent that the parent can be identified, out of separately trained networks, across a range of prune ratios. It defines 'prune potential' as the largest prune ratio at which the pruned network keeps its original performance. Prune potential varies greatly across tasks and is much lower on harder inference tasks, including under noise or distribution shift. Matching test accuracy does not imply matching the parent's function off-distribution.
items.relevance: Pruned g sit measurably closer to f than independent retrains do, which is what the compression bound needs. How much compression keeps agreement high depends on the task, so the surrogate's size has to be chosen per task. Off-distribution disagreement does not matter for us, because Pr[f != g] is measured under the known D_X.

items.citation: Cenk Baykal, Lucas Liebenwein, Igor Gilitschenski, Dan Feldman, Daniela Rus. 'Data-Dependent Coresets for Compressing Neural Networks with Applications to Generalization Bounds.' ICLR 2019, arXiv 1804.05345. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets of the abstract and OpenReview listing.
items.finding: Sensitivity-based importance sampling over a trained fully connected network's parameters. Weights are sampled with probability proportional to an empirical sensitivity estimated from a small batch of inputs, and reweighted, keeping high-importance weights and dropping redundant ones. The result is a sparse network whose output provably approximates the original's with high probability over inputs from the data distribution. The paper gives bounds on size versus accuracy and derives generalization bounds from them. Experiments use LeNet-300-100 on MNIST, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, and Fashion-MNIST, against uniform, norm-threshold and norm-importance sampling baselines. I could not confirm the exact compression ratios. A figure of about 90% compression of LeNet-300-100 belongs to the follow-up 'Data-Independent Neural Pruning via Coresets' (Mussay et al., ICLR 2020), not this paper.
items.relevance: This is the closest existing work to the subsampling idea in the request. It is a polynomial-time, Maurey or importance-sampling style construction of a small g with a high-probability guarantee that g's output tracks f's on D_X, and it already feeds a generalization bound. The required sample size grows with the total sensitivity, which can be large for trained networks. Measuring that quantity on our networks tells us whether subsampling gives a short enough g.

items.citation: Lei Jimmy Ba, Rich Caruana. 'Do Deep Nets Really Need to be Deep?' NeurIPS 2014, arXiv 1312.6184. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; numbers from snippets of the paper and summaries.
items.finding: Shallow single-hidden-layer nets trained to regress a deep teacher's logits ('mimic' training) on TIMIT match much deeper nets. A shallow mimic net with 8k ReLU units, with a parameter count similar to the DNN (about 12M per a review), reaches 21.6% phone error rate versus the DNN's 21.9%. A 400k-unit mimic net (about 180M parameters) reaches 20.0% versus the CNN's 19.5%. The same shallow nets trained directly on the labels are 1.4-2% worse than the DNN and 3.5-4.1% worse than the CNN. The paper reports accuracy, not teacher-student agreement.
items.relevance: In this setting the obstacle to a small or simple g is how it is trained, not its capacity: the same shallow architecture fails on labels and succeeds when fitted to f's logits. So fitting g to f's real-valued outputs, which we can query without limit when D_X is known, is the right objective for finding a close g. Whether this gives low Pr[f != g], as opposed to matching accuracy, was not measured.

items.citation: Gregor Urban, Krzysztof J. Geras, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou, Ozlem Aslan, Shengjie Wang, Abdelrahman Mohamed, Matthai Philipose, Matt Richardson, Rich Caruana. 'Do Deep Convolutional Nets Really Need to be Deep and Convolutional?' ICLR 2017, arXiv 1603.05691. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets.
items.finding: On CIFAR-10, shallow students trained to mimic a 16-model deep convolutional 'super teacher' ensemble cannot match deep convolutional accuracy unless they have several convolutional layers. This holds even with distillation, Bayesian-optimized hyperparameters (Spearmint, 18 hyperparameters per model), and shallow students up to 30x the teacher's parameters. The shallow convolutional students stay several points below a teacher that is itself below the state of the art. An auto-generated summary gives about 74.3% for the best MLP student and 87.3% for a 1-conv-layer student; I could not check these numbers.
items.relevance: Capacity does bind when the student's architecture lacks the teacher's inductive structure. The search for g should therefore range over the same family as f (sparse or narrow versions of f's architecture, as in subsampling), not over arbitrary 'simple' shallow models.

items.citation: Lucas Beyer, Xiaohua Zhai, Amelie Royer, Larisa Markeeva, Rohan Anil, Alexander Kolesnikov. 'Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent.' CVPR 2022, arXiv 2106.05237. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets.
items.finding: Distillation works best as 'function matching': teacher and student see identical, aggressively augmented views, and training runs for a very large number of epochs. Distilling from precomputed teacher targets works much worse. With this recipe a ResNet-50 student distilled from a BiT ResNet-152x2 teacher reaches 82.8% ImageNet top-1, 4.4 points above a ResNet-50 trained normally. A snippet mentions schedules of up to 9,600 epochs; I did not confirm the exact count.
items.relevance: Long optimization keeps improving distillation quality, which again says optimization rather than capacity is the bottleneck. With known D_X, the analogue of 'consistent views' is fresh samples labeled by f at every step, at no cost. The price is that compute is the knob, and the paper shows how large that compute can get.

items.citation: Dan Busbridge, Amitis Shidani, Floris Weers, Jason Ramapuram, Etai Littwin, Russ Webb. 'Distillation Scaling Laws.' ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.08606. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets of the ICML page and arXiv PDF.
items.finding: The paper fits a scaling law for distilled student cross-entropy as a function of student size, teacher quality and the compute split between them. Commentary gives the scale as students of 143M-12.6B parameters; I did not confirm this. It explains the 'capacity gap', where a stronger teacher can yield a weaker student, as a gap in learning capacity covering both hypothesis space and ability to optimize. The gap is not a function of the size ratio alone. Distillation beats supervised learning up to a compute level that scales predictably with student size. With enough data or compute, distillation cannot give lower cross-entropy than supervised learning.
items.relevance: This is a modern, quantitative statement that how well a small g can track f depends on student capacity and optimization compute together. It gives a prior on how agreement should scale with surrogate size and distillation compute. It also suggests that when f is much larger than g, an intermediate model (as in teacher-assistant distillation) can help.

items.citation: Vaishnavh Nagarajan, Aditya Krishna Menon, Srinadh Bhojanapalli, Hossein Mobahi, Sanjiv Kumar. 'On student-teacher deviations in distillation: does it pay to disobey?' NeurIPS 2023, arXiv 2301.12923. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets of the abstract.
items.finding: Student-teacher deviations are systematic, not random: students exaggerate the teacher's confidence levels. This holds across image and language tasks and even in self-distillation, so it is not just a capacity mismatch. The authors trace it to distillation amplifying gradient descent's implicit bias, which converges faster along the top eigendirections of the data. The same exaggerated regularization explains both the confidence exaggeration and the better generalization.
items.relevance: Disagreement between a distilled g and f should concentrate on f's low-margin inputs. This matches the PIE finding, and means that certifying Pr[f != g] by sampling should be straightforward, but driving it to zero is hard. Matching logits or margins (not just argmax) on low-confidence regions is where an improved search should spend its effort.

items.finding: Soft-target distillation at temperature T. On MNIST, a dropout-regularized 2x1200 ReLU teacher makes 67 test errors, and a 2x800 net trained normally makes 146. The same 2x800 net distilled at T = 20 makes 74. When digit 3 is omitted from the transfer set, the distilled net makes 206 errors, 133 of them on the 1010 test 3s, and 109 errors (14 on 3s) after a bias adjustment. Agreement with the teacher is not reported; only error counts are.
items.relevance: This is the baseline method for fitting g to f. Error counts close to the teacher's (74 vs 67 out of 10,000) mean the agreement gap is at most about 0.7% plus the overlap of the two error sets. In easy, low-noise regimes a much smaller network gets very close to f, which is the condition under which the oracle bound becomes tight.

items.finding: Large ensembles (ensemble selection over hundreds of models) are compressed into a single neural network trained to mimic the ensemble on a large synthetic transfer set, across eight binary classification problems. The synthetic inputs come from MUNGE, which perturbs and recombines training points to approximate the input distribution, and are labeled by the ensemble. A secondary source reports the mimic nets perform comparably while being about 1000x smaller and faster. The authors stress that the synthetic data must match the true input distribution.
items.relevance: This is the original demonstration that the amount of transfer data is the main lever for making a small mimic match a big model. When D_X is known, as with uniform Boolean inputs, unlimited correctly distributed transfer data is free, so the one limitation they had to work around (estimating D_X) does not apply to us.

items.citation: Enric Boix-Adsera. 'Towards a theory of model distillation.' arXiv 2403.09053 (2024). UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets of the abstract. The poly(d, 2^r) runtime is quoted from a later citing paper, arXiv 2605.20074.
items.finding: The paper defines PAC-distillation, analogous to PAC-learning: given access to a trained model, output a simpler model that approximates it with high probability under the input distribution. It shows how to efficiently distill neural networks into succinct, explicit decision trees when such trees exist, using the 'linear representation hypothesis' that the network's internal activations linearly encode the relevant features. It proves that distillation can be much cheaper than learning from scratch, and partly characterizes its complexity. A later paper says the framework yields a PAC-distillation algorithm for depth-r decision trees in poly(d, 2^r) time, where learning such trees from examples is not known to be possible in less than d^O(r) time. I did not confirm the exact theorem statements.
items.relevance: This is the most direct theoretical answer to the compute question. White-box access to f's internals can turn the exponential search for a short g (here a decision tree or junta) into a polynomial one, under a representation assumption. Black-box distillation cannot do this in general. It supports using f's weights and activations (subsampling neurons, reading off features), not just its input-output behavior. Note: the arXiv id is 2403.09053; the URL field has a typo, the correct link is https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09053.

items.citation: Abhishek Panigrahi, Bingbin Liu, Sadhika Malladi, Andrej Risteski, Surbhi Goel. 'Progressive distillation induces an implicit curriculum.' ICLR 2025, arXiv 2410.05464. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; details from snippets.
items.finding: On sparse parity, which uses uniform Boolean inputs, distilling from a sequence of the teacher's intermediate checkpoints provably improves the student's sample complexity over one-shot distillation from the final teacher and over learning directly from data. A secondary summary describes the gain as exponential to polynomial in the support size; I did not confirm this. The curriculum, in which easy subtasks reveal the parity's support coordinates, is available only from intermediate checkpoints, not the converged one. The most useful checkpoint is in the middle of the phase transition. Analogous effects appear for Transformers on PCFGs and in BERT pretraining.
items.relevance: This is a cautionary result for Boolean tasks. Black-box access to the final f under uniform inputs gives roughly no more than a label oracle, so finding a small g close to f can be as hard as learning the target, for example n^k for k-sparse parity. Cheap search for g has to use more than f's input-output map: its training trajectory or its weights, as in subsampling.

report.synthesis:
Access caveat: I could not open any paper page. WebFetch failed DNS for arxiv.org and proceedings.neurips.cc, and curl through the proxy also failed for export.arxiv.org, openreview.net, papers.nips.cc, semanticscholar.org, proceedings.mlr.press, openaccess.thecvf.com and dl.acm.org. Every item is therefore UNVERIFIED (verified=false). The titles, authors, venues and the stated findings and numbers come from search-result snippets, and some from secondary summaries; each item says which. To check them, arxiv.org (and ideally proceedings.neurips.cc and openreview.net) has to be allowed in the session's network settings. One URL has a typo: Boix-Adsera is arXiv 2403.09053 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09053), not 2403.09653.

What the literature says for our question:

(1) Is the gap between a small g and a trained f usually capacity or optimization? Mostly optimization when g is in f's own family and is trained to imitate f.
- Stanton et al. 2021: same-architecture self-distillation, where g = f is in the search space, still leaves large disagreement. This holds even on the distillation data itself. The best CIFAR-100 test top-1 agreement is about 85%.
- In the same paper, agreement jumps only when the student is initialized close to the teacher's weights (lambda >= 0.375).
- More fresh transfer data raises test agreement but lowers train agreement, and longer schedules or other optimizers change little.
- Beyer et al. 2022: very long, consistent 'function matching' keeps improving the student, which is again an optimization effect.
- Pruning-based compressions start from f's weights and stay functionally close. Evci et al. find lottery tickets relearn the pruning solution in the same basin. Liebenwein et al. find pruned networks identifiable as their parent's. Hooker et al. find 90%-sparse ResNet-50 within about 3 points top-1, with disagreement concentrated on a few atypical 'PIE' inputs. Nagarajan et al. find deviations are systematic, concentrated where f has low confidence.

(2) Capacity does bind in some cases.
- Urban et al. 2017: shallow students without convolutional depth cannot match deep CNNs on CIFAR-10 even at 30x the parameters.
- Busbridge et al. 2025: the 'capacity gap' combines hypothesis space and optimization ability.
- Ba & Caruana 2014, Hinton et al. 2015 and Bucilua et al. 2006 show that a much smaller network fitted to f's soft outputs on lots of correctly distributed data comes very close to f in easier regimes (MNIST 74 vs 67 errors, TIMIT 21.6 vs 21.9% phone error rate). These papers report accuracy, not agreement.

(3) A baseline any g must beat: by Jiang et al. 2022, an independently retrained network disagrees with f at about err(f). So a g not tailored to f gives a bound of at least about 2*err(f), and the useful regime is Pr[f != g] much smaller than err(f).

(4) Compute. Known D_X removes the data bottleneck (unlimited f-labeled fresh samples, as in Bucilua's synthetic transfer set), but not the optimization bottleneck.
- The positive results on making the search for g cheap all use white-box access to f.
- Coreset or importance sampling of f's weights (Baykal et al. 2019) gives a polynomial-time g with a high-probability output-approximation guarantee on D_X and a generalization bound. Its size scales with the total sensitivity, which is the quantity to measure.
- Boix-Adsera 2024 shows distillation into decision trees can be done efficiently under a linear-representation assumption, and that distillation can be much cheaper than learning; one citing paper gives poly(d, 2^r) for depth-r trees versus d^O(r) for learning.
- The negative side for Boolean tasks: Panigrahi et al. 2025 show that for sparse parity, one-shot distillation from the final f gives no sample-complexity benefit over learning from labels. The benefit comes only from intermediate checkpoints. So black-box search for g can be as hard as learning.

Recommendation: initialize g as an importance-subsampled sparse or narrow copy of f. Score neurons or weights by sensitivity, Maurey style. Then fine-tune g on fresh D_X samples to match f's logits, and certify Pr[f != g] with independent samples. Charge L(g) as the subsample indices plus the quantized weights. This uses the near-f initialization that Stanton et al. and Evci et al. show is what makes agreement reachable, and avoids exponential search. Two failure modes to report: the total sensitivity may be too large for a short code, and parity-like targets, where only trajectory or weight information helps.
