items.finding: With membership queries under the uniform distribution, the algorithm finds every Fourier coefficient with |f^(S)| >= theta in poly(n, 1/theta) time. If ||f^||_1 <= L, keeping the coefficients of magnitude >= eps/L gives a polynomial p with ||f - p||_2^2 <= eps and at most L^2/eps terms. The class {||f^||_1 <= s} is therefore learnable with queries in poly(n, s, 1/eps) time. This includes poly-size decision trees, since a size-s tree has L1 <= s.
items.relevance: This is the canonical polynomial-time compressor for our setting: query access plus uniform inputs. The output g = sign(p) has an explicit description of about (L^2/eps)(n + O(log(L/eps))) bits, and Pr[f != g] <= ||f - p||_2^2 can be certified by sampling. It gives a certified upper bound on K_eps(f) in polynomial time whenever the trained network has small spectral L1 norm. Whether trained networks do is an empirical question; the bound degrades as (L1)^2.

items.citation: Oded Goldreich, Leonid A. Levin. A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions. STOC 1989, pp. 25-32. DOI 10.1145/73007.73010. UNVERIFIED: page not opened.
items.finding: The paper proves that <p, x> is a hard-core bit for f(p, x) = (p, g(x)). The algorithmic core, standardly read as list-decoding the Hadamard code, takes query access to any h: {0,1}^n -> {+-1} and outputs, in poly(n, 1/theta) time, a list containing every parity chi_S with correlation >= theta. It is the subroutine inside Kushilevitz-Mansour and Jackson.
items.relevance: This is the poly-time primitive that replaces exponential search over the 2^n parities. It is the reason Fourier-dictionary compression of a trained Boolean network is cheap. Each round costs poly(n, 1/theta) queries to f, and each query is one forward pass.

items.citation: Jeffrey C. Jackson. An Efficient Membership-Query Algorithm for Learning DNF with Respect to the Uniform Distribution. FOCS 1994; J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 55, 1997. DOI 10.1006/jcss.1997.1533. UNVERIFIED: page not opened.
items.finding: The Harmonic Sieve combines Goldreich-Levin/KM heavy-parity finding with boosting. It learns s-term DNF under the uniform distribution with membership queries in poly(n, s, 1/eps) time. Its hypothesis is a threshold (majority) of polynomially many parities, so it also properly learns thresholds-of-parities (Bshouty-Jackson). One secondary source gives sample complexity ~O(n s^4 / eps^8), later improved to ~O(r s^2 / eps^4).
items.relevance: Boosting over GL-found parities still produces a short, explicit hypothesis whose length is polynomial in n, s and 1/eps. It works for targets with large L1 norm, as long as f weakly correlates with some parity under every smooth reweighting. This makes it a stronger efficient Occam compressor than plain KM for Boolean tasks.

items.citation: Parikshit Gopalan, Adam Tauman Kalai, Adam R. Klivans. Agnostically Learning Decision Trees. STOC 2008. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; abstract seen via search snippets of the MSR page and an NYU seminar abstract.
items.finding: Given black-box query access to an arbitrary f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1}, the algorithm finds h whose agreement with f is within eps of the best size-t decision tree, under the uniform distribution, in poly(n, t, 1/eps) time. The method is approximate gradient projection over the L1 ball in 2^n dimensions, implemented with KM-style coefficient finding. As I recall, h is a threshold of a sparse polynomial with poly(t/eps) terms, but I did not see this confirmed.
items.relevance: This is the agnostic version of our search, solved in polynomial time for the decision-tree dictionary. If the trained network is opt-close to some size-t tree, we efficiently get g with Pr[f != g] <= opt + eps and a description length polynomial in t/eps (times n). It shows that the closeness assumption, f close to simple, can be exploited without knowing the simple function, for this class.

items.citation: Guy Blanc, Jane Lange, Mingda Qiao, Li-Yang Tan. Properly Learning Decision Trees in Almost Polynomial Time. FOCS 2021; Journal of the ACM 69(6), 2022. arXiv:2109.00637. UNVERIFIED: arXiv not reachable.
items.finding: A membership-query algorithm properly and agnostically learns size-s decision trees under the uniform distribution on {+-1}^n in n^{O(log log n)} time. The previous best, even in the realizable case, was n^{O(log n)} (Ehrenfeucht-Haussler). The output is itself a decision tree, close to the best size-s tree.
items.relevance: Proper output means g is literally a small tree with L(g) of about s log n bits, which is exactly what the Occam term needs. With uniform inputs, near-optimal-size compression to the tree dictionary is almost polynomial, not exponential. Contrast this with the NP-hardness in the Koch-Strassle-Tan item.

items.citation: Caleb Koch, Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan. Properly Learning Decision Trees with Queries Is NP-Hard. FOCS 2023. arXiv:2307.04093. Follow-up: Koch, Strassle, Tan, Superconstant Inapproximability of Decision Tree Learning, COLT 2024 (PMLR 247:2979-3010), arXiv:2407.01402. UNVERIFIED: arXiv not reachable.
items.finding: There is an absolute constant eps > 0 such that properly PAC-learning decision trees is NP-hard even with membership queries; earlier hardness covered random examples only. This resolves questions of Bshouty (1993) and Feldman (2016). The COLT 2024 follow-up shows that a learner outputting a tree of size 2^{O(r)} s would solve SAT in randomized time ~O(r n^2) t(n^{O(r)}, 2^{O(r)}), giving superconstant inapproximability under stronger assumptions. The quoted theorem uses query access plus random examples from a distribution D.
items.relevance: Exact or near-exact minimum-description search is NP-hard even for the simplest dictionary, with queries. My inference, not stated in the snippets: the hard D must be non-uniform, because under the uniform distribution the BLQT algorithm runs in n^{O(log log n)}. The known-uniform-input setting the user highlighted is therefore the favourable case.

items.citation: Michael Kharitonov. Cryptographic Hardness of Distribution-Specific Learning. STOC 1993, pp. 372-381 (DOI 10.1145/167088.167197); journal version: Cryptographic Lower Bounds for Learnability of Boolean Functions on the Uniform Distribution, JCSS 1995. Related: Moni Naor, Omer Reingold, Number-Theoretic Constructions of Efficient Pseudo-Random Functions, FOCS 1997 / JACM 51(2), 2004 (PRFs in TC0 under DDH or factoring). UNVERIFIED: pages not opened.
items.finding: Assuming factoring Blum integers is hard, Boolean formulas (NC1) and constant-depth polynomial-size threshold circuits (TC0) are not even weakly predictable under the uniform distribution, even with membership queries. Under a stronger factoring assumption, the tight lower bound for AC0 matches the quasi-polynomial Linial-Mansour-Nisan Fourier algorithm. Naor-Reingold give PRFs computable in TC0. By Valiant's (1984) observation on GGM PRFs, TC0 is then not learnable with queries under the uniform distribution.
items.relevance: Constant-depth threshold circuits are small sign-activation neural networks. With only black-box (query) access to f, no poly-time procedure can find any efficiently evaluable g with error 1/2 - 1/poly for all small networks f. This rules out a general distillation-by-querying scheme with worst-case guarantees. Note that in the PRF case f is itself small, so the hardness is about finding g, not about K_eps(f) being large. An efficient scheme must therefore use the weights (white-box) or properties typical of trained networks.

items.citation: Shuichi Hirahara. NP-Hardness of Learning Programs and Partial MCSP. FOCS 2022; ECCC TR22-119. UNVERIFIED: ECCC not reachable; abstract content seen via search snippets.
items.finding: Under randomized polynomial-time many-one reductions, it is NP-hard to decide whether some small, time-bounded program is consistent with a given set of labeled samples, i.e. to learn programs (Ko's MINLT, studied 1990-91). Partial MCSP, MKTP* and MINKT* are also NP-hard. The proof is non-relativizing and so overcomes Ko's 1991 barrier, which showed that no relativizing proof exists. It uses Nisan-Wigderson-style PRGs as one-time encryption and conditional Kolmogorov complexity.
items.relevance: Finding the shortest program, or even a short time-bounded one, consistent with f on a sample is worst-case NP-hard. So the step 'find g agreeing with f on m sampled points with near-minimal L(g)' cannot be efficient in general. The hardness is for the random-example (partial truth table) setting; the queries/uniform setting is not directly covered.

items.citation: Halley Goldberg, Valentine Kabanets. Witness Encryption and NP-Hardness of Learning. CCC 2025, LIPIcs vol. 339, 34:1-34:43; ECCC TR25-070. UNVERIFIED: page not opened.
items.finding: Certain formulations of NP-hardness of (agnostic) PAC learning are equivalent to the existence of witness encryption for NP. Unconditionally, the paper extends Hirahara 2022 to ordinary Boolean circuits, showing NP-hardness of semi-proper learning, where the hypothesis may be somewhat larger than the target class. It also draws consequences for private- and public-key cryptography.
items.relevance: Semi-proper is exactly the Occam regime: we accept L(g) somewhat above K_eps(f). This shows that allowing slack in description length does not, by itself, make the circuit-dictionary search tractable in the worst case.

items.citation: Daniel Buchfuhrer, Christopher Umans. The Complexity of Boolean Formula Minimization. ICALP 2008; JCSS 77(1), 2011 (DOI 10.1016/j.jcss.2010.06.011). Christopher Umans. The Minimum Equivalent DNF Problem and Shortest Implicants. FOCS 1998, pp. 556-563; JCSS 63(4):597-611, 2001. UNVERIFIED: pages not opened.
items.finding: Minimum Equivalent Expression (given a formula, find a minimum equivalent formula), a Garey-Johnson open problem, is Sigma2P-complete under Turing reductions; so is the depth-k version for every k >= 3. Umans: Minimum Equivalent DNF is Sigma2P-complete. Shortest implicant is Sigma2P-hard to approximate within n^{1/2-eps} for formula input and n^{1-eps} for circuit input. Dick-Umans 2009 give n^{1/3-eps} and n^{1/2-eps} for DNF variants.
items.relevance: White-box exact minimization is Sigma2-hard, but the extra coNP layer comes from requiring exact equivalence. In our eps-approximate, uniform-distribution version, agreement is checked by sampling, a BPP verifier. That collapses the problem to roughly NP-search ('exists short g that passes a sampling test'). So for us the relevant barrier is NP and crypto-style hardness, not Sigma2. This reduction is my own reasoning; the papers do not state it.

items.citation: Russell Impagliazzo, Valentine Kabanets, Ilya Volkovich. The Power of Natural Properties as Oracles. CCC 2018 (LIPIcs CCC.2018.7). Also: Synergy Between Circuit Obfuscation and Circuit Minimization, APPROX/RANDOM 2023 (LIPIcs vol. 275, art. 31; ECCC TR23-079). UNVERIFIED: pages not opened.
items.finding: 2018: if indistinguishability obfuscation (iO) exists, then MCSP is in ZPP iff NP = ZPP; iO gives a non-black-box randomized reduction from SAT to MCSP. 2023: with computationally-secure perfect iO, MCSP in BPP iff NP = ZPP (ECCC version), and given a circuit C, the lexicographically smallest equivalent circuit is computable in PH. Related: Mazor-Pass (CCC 2024) show that, assuming iO and subexponentially secure one-way functions (OWFs), a gap version of MCSP is not NP-hard under randomized Levin reductions.
items.relevance: This is the obfuscation link for white-box access. Obfuscation ties circuit minimization to NP-hardness. A caveat from my own reasoning: iO alone does not obviously stop one from extracting a small equivalent circuit, since iO is 'best-possible obfuscation' and a padded small circuit leaks its small core. I found no paper showing that iO makes approximate minimization of a circuit given as input hard. Treat white-box hardness as open, not established.

items.citation: Yanyi Liu, Rafael Pass. On One-way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity. FOCS 2020; arXiv:2009.11514; IACR ePrint 2020/423. Related: Liu, Pass, Characterizing Derandomization Through Hardness of Levin-Kolmogorov Complexity, CCC 2022 (LIPIcs CCC.2022.35). UNVERIFIED: arXiv not reachable.
items.finding: One-way functions exist iff, for every polynomial t(n) >= (1+eps)n, K^t is mildly hard on average over uniform n-bit strings: there is a polynomial p such that no PPT algorithm computes K^t correctly on more than a 1 - 1/p(n) fraction of inputs. CCC 2022: for large constants c, prBPP = prP iff computing conditional Levin Kt(x | z) is hard in a specified sense.
items.relevance: Efficient approximate computation of the shortest time-bounded description, on average, is equivalent to breaking OWFs. A generic efficient search for near-shortest g therefore exists only in a world without cryptography. Any practical scheme must exploit special structure of trained networks, such as low influence, Fourier concentration, or sparse sub-networks, rather than generic compression.

items.citation: Shuichi Hirahara, Rahul Ilango, Ryan Williams. Beating Brute Force for Compression Problems. STOC 2024, pp. 659-670 (DOI 10.1145/3618260.3649778); ECCC TR23-171. Related: Noam Mazor, Rafael Pass, ITCS 2024 (non-uniform Perebor conjecture for K^t is false). UNVERIFIED: pages not opened.
items.finding: For any compression problem with decoder time t, there are circuits of size about 2^{4l/5} poly(t) that find a description of length l whenever one exists. Brute force costs about 2^l t. This covers MCSP (circuits of size 2^{4s/5} poly) and K^t. The construction adapts Fiat-Naor function inversion with hashing; it is non-uniform (circuits with preprocessing), not a uniform algorithm.
items.relevance: The best known generic speed-up over exhaustive search over g only shaves the exponent from l to 0.8 l, and only non-uniformly. For surrogates with L(g) of hundreds to thousands of bits, generic search stays hopeless. Efficiency must come from restricting the dictionary (Fourier, junta, tree, subsampled network), not from smarter generic search.

items.citation: Leonid A. Levin. Universal Sequential Search Problems. Problems of Information Transmission 9(3):115-116 (English translation pp. 265-266), 1973. UNVERIFIED: page not opened; the 2^{l(p)} t_p form is the standard later restatement, also given in arXiv:1702.03152.
items.finding: Levin search interleaves all programs and finds a solution in time about 2^{l(p*)} t*, where p* is the fastest-solving program of length l(p*). This motivates Levin complexity Kt(x) = min_p {|p| + log t_p(x)}: Levin search computes a Kt-optimal description in time about 2^{Kt}. Allender, Buhrman, Koucky, van Melkebeek, Ronneburger (FOCS 2002 / SICOMP 2006) show that R_Kt is EXP-complete under P/poly truth-table reductions and under NP-Turing reductions.
items.relevance: This formalizes the user's worry. The natural algorithm for a computable Kt-style Occam bound costs exponential in L(g) plus log of the evaluation time. The Kt bound is only computable for tiny descriptions, and its decision version is EXP-hard under reductions. A Kt-based certificate is only practical if the dictionary is restricted or L(g) is tens of bits.

items.citation: Esty Kelman, Guy Kindler, Noam Lifshitz, Dor Minzer, Muli Safra. Towards a Proof of the Fourier-Entropy Conjecture? FOCS 2020; Geometric and Functional Analysis 2020. arXiv:1911.10579. UNVERIFIED: arXiv not reachable.
items.finding: The Fourier spectrum of any constant-variance Boolean f concentrates on 2^{O(I[f] log I[f])} characters, where I[f] is total influence. This improves Friedgut's junta theorem, under which f is eps-close to a 2^{O(I/eps)}-junta. Consequence: functions with total influence <= K are agnostically learnable with membership queries in 2^{O(K log K)} time, and those with I = O(log n / log log n) in poly(n) time.
items.relevance: This gives a compression guarantee and search algorithm indexed by a quantity we can measure cheaply by sampling the trained network: I[f] = sum_i Pr_x[f(x) != f(x^{(i)})], at cost about n forward passes per sample. If trained networks on Boolean tasks have small total influence, this yields an efficient certified surrogate whose description length is set by I[f], not by network size. It is a concrete, testable route to sub-exponential compute.

report.synthesis:
Access caveat: none of the source pages could be opened. WebFetch returned DNS failures for arxiv.org, eccc.weizmann.ac.il, drops.dagstuhl.de, dblp.org and semanticscholar.org. curl from Bash got proxy 403s for those hosts and also for proceedings.mlr.press and openreview.net. Every item is therefore marked UNVERIFIED (verified=false). Each one is reconstructed from several consistent search-result snippets of its abstract or bibliographic page. Those hosts must be allowed in the session's network settings before the items can be checked against the papers.

1. Worst case, finding a near-shortest g is hard, and generic search stays exponential. Several independent results point the same way:
- Hirahara 2022 (NP-hardness of learning programs and of partial MCSP) and Goldberg-Kabanets 2025 (semi-proper circuit learning) show that finding a short program or circuit consistent with samples of f is NP-hard, even with some slack in hypothesis size.
- Kharitonov 1993 and Naor-Reingold PRFs in TC0 show that with only query access, small constant-depth threshold networks cannot even be weakly approximated in poly time under the uniform distribution, assuming factoring or DDH is hard. Black-box distillation of an arbitrary small network therefore has no worst-case guarantee.
- Liu-Pass 2020: average-case approximation of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity is efficient iff one-way functions do not exist.
- Hirahara-Ilango-Williams 2024: the best generic speed-up over brute force is 2^{0.8 L} instead of 2^L, and only non-uniformly. Levin search and Kt make the 2^{L(g)} cost explicit.

2. Exact white-box minimization is even harder (Sigma2-complete: Umans; Buchfuhrer-Umans), but that extra layer does not apply to us. In the eps-approximate, known-distribution version, agreement Pr[f != g] is certified by sampling, so the problem is NP-search with a BPP verifier. The relevant barriers are the NP-hardness and crypto results in point 1. I found no paper showing that obfuscation makes approximate minimization of a given circuit hard. Impagliazzo-Kabanets-Volkovich only tie MCSP to NP under iO, and by my own reasoning iO's best-possible-obfuscation property does not obviously block extraction. So whether the white-box case is hard looks open.

3. Restricted dictionaries with queries under uniform inputs are efficient, and that is the user's setting:
- Goldreich-Levin and Kushilevitz-Mansour: find heavy Fourier coefficients in poly(n, 1/theta). The result is a certified sparse g with about L1^2/eps terms.
- Jackson: thresholds of parities and DNF in poly time.
- Gopalan-Kalai-Klivans: agnostic decision trees in poly(n, t, 1/eps).
- Blanc-Lange-Qiao-Tan: proper agnostic decision trees in n^{O(log log n)}.
- Kelman et al.: total influence K gives agnostic learning in 2^{O(K log K)}, and is poly(n) for K = O(log n / log log n).
- Koch-Strassle-Tan show proper decision-tree learning with queries is NP-hard. I infer it must use a non-uniform distribution, since it would otherwise contradict Blanc-Lange-Qiao-Tan. That makes known-uniform inputs exactly the favourable case.
- A standard fact I did not verify: k-juntas are learnable with membership queries in poly(n, 2^k) time. From random examples alone the best is about n^{omega k/(omega+1)} (Mossel-O'Donnell-Servedio 2004).

4. Implications for the user's plan:
- (a) A cheap first step is to measure, by sampling the trained network, the statistics that index these efficient algorithms: total influence, the heavy Fourier coefficients found by Goldreich-Levin, and noise sensitivity. Each yields a constructive, certified surrogate in poly time, so a certified upper bound on K_eps(f) without exponential search. Whether trained networks are close to such simple functions is then an empirical, checkable question. The literature here gives the tools, not the answer.
- (b) Neuron or weight subsampling (Maurey, Barron, importance sampling) is a white-box, randomized, poly-time compressor whose output size is controlled by a norm of f's own weights, such as path or variation norm. It is not trying to find the shortest g, so none of the hardness results above apply to it. It also escapes the TC0-PRF barrier because it uses the weights, not just queries. Its weakness is the reverse: no optimality guarantee relative to K_eps(f).
- The complexity literature suggests combining them: norm-based subsampling to shrink the network cheaply, then dictionary-restricted search (Fourier, influence, decision trees) for further compression, each step certified by sampling.

Additional pointers seen only in search results, not itemised:
- Carmosino-Impagliazzo-Kabanets-Kolokolova, CCC 2016: AC0[p] is learnable with membership queries under the uniform distribution in quasi-poly time, derived from natural proofs.
- Karchmer, ALT 2024 (arXiv:2311.06690): agnostic membership-query learning with nontrivial savings for sublinear-size circuits of low-degree threshold gates (gates resembling neurons).
- Liu-Mazor-Pass, ITCS 2025: hardness of white-box learning characterizes public-key encryption; the black-box version characterizes OWFs.
- Goldwasser-Kim-Vaikuntanathan-Zamir, FOCS 2022: white-box-undetectable backdoors in networks. These only affect a negligible input fraction, so they do not threaten sampling-certified eps-agreement.
- Board-Pitt, STOC 1990: for classes closed under exception lists, PAC learnability implies an Occam (compression) algorithm.
- Ko, SICOMP 1991: there is no relativizing proof that learning minimum time-bounded Turing machines is NP-hard.

checks.corrected_finding: The STOC 1993 paper is confirmed: pp. 372-381, DOI 10.1145/167088.167197, PDF at cis.upenn.edu (not openable here). Its abstract says that weakly learning Boolean formulas and constant-depth threshold circuits on the uniform distribution, even with membership queries, is as hard as factoring Blum integers, inverting RSA or deciding quadratic residuosity. The hardness extends to every 'non-trivial' distribution, and learnability is characterized by the distribution's Renyi entropy. Under a stronger, subexponential factoring assumption it gives tight superpolynomial lower bounds for depth-d circuits (AC0) on the uniform distribution with membership queries, matching known (LMN) upper bounds. Correction: the JCSS 1995 paper, 'Cryptographic Lower Bounds for Learnability of Boolean Functions on the Uniform Distribution' (DOI 10.1006/jcss.1995.1046), is the journal version of Kharitonov's COLT 1992 paper of that title, not of STOC 1993. Also, STOC 1993 already gives TC0 hardness with queries, so Naor-Reingold is not needed for that conclusion. Naor-Reingold is confirmed: FOCS 1997; JACM 51(2):231-262, 2004, DOI 10.1145/972639.972643; PRFs in TC0 from DDH or factoring, with learning theory listed as an application.

checks.citation: Shuichi Hirahara. NP-Hardness of Learning Programs and Partial MCSP. FOCS 2022; ECCC TR22-119.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search snippets of the FOCS PDF and the ECCC abstract (ECCC is blocked here). FOCS 2022, DOI 10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00095; ECCC TR22-119, Aug 2022. The paper proves NP-hardness of learning efficient programs under randomized polynomial-time reductions. This overcomes Ko's barrier (COLT'90 / SICOMP'91: no relativizing proof exists), and the proof is provably non-relativizing. It also proves NP-hardness of Partial MCSP, MINKT* and MKTP*. Techniques: Kolmogorov complexity, quantifying a program's 'knowledge' via conditional Kolmogorov complexity, and Nisan-Wigderson-type generators. Widely noted, e.g. Computational Complexity blog 'result of the year'. The agent's caveat that this is the random-example (partial truth table) setting, not queries, is consistent with the problem definitions.

checks.citation: Halley Goldberg, Valentine Kabanets. Witness Encryption and NP-Hardness of Learning. CCC 2025, LIPIcs vol. 339, 34:1-34:43; ECCC TR25-070.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search snippets of the Dagstuhl and ECCC abstracts (both blocked for direct fetch). CCC 2025, LIPIcs 339, pp. 34:1-34:43; ECCC TR25-070 (June 2025). Certain formulations of NP-hardness of learning characterize the existence of witness encryption for NP. In one formulation, witness encryption for an NP language corresponds to a half-Levin reduction to Computational Gap Learning (CGL). Consequence: if CGL is NP-hard under such a reduction, then NP not in BPP implies infinitely-often public-key encryption. The paper also gives unconditional NP-hardness results for agnostic PAC learning, extending Hirahara (2022) to standard Boolean circuits, i.e. NP-hardness of 'semi-proper' learning. NP-hardness of fully improper learning of circuits is left open. The exact size slack in the 'semi-proper' definition was not confirmed, so the claim that it 'is exactly the Occam regime' is the agent's interpretation.

checks.citation: Daniel Buchfuhrer, Christopher Umans. The Complexity of Boolean Formula Minimization. ICALP 2008; JCSS 77(1), 2011. Christopher Umans. The Minimum Equivalent DNF Problem and Shortest Implicants. FOCS 1998; JCSS 63(4), 2001.
checks.corrected_finding: Correction: the first author is David Buchfuhrer, not Daniel. Otherwise confirmed from search results. Buchfuhrer-Umans: JCSS 77(1):142-153, 2011, DOI 10.1016/j.jcss.2010.06.011; ICALP 2008 pp. 24-35, Track A best paper. Minimum Equivalent Expression (open problem in Garey-Johnson) is Sigma2P-complete under Turing reductions, and so is the depth-k version for all k >= 3. Umans FOCS 1998 / JCSS 2001: Minimum Equivalent DNF is Sigma2P-complete (Stockmeyer's conjecture). Shortest Implicant is Sigma2P-complete for formula input, Sigma2P-hard to approximate within n^{1/2-eps} for formulas and n^{1-eps} for circuits. For DNF input it is not Sigma2P-complete unless the hierarchy collapses. 'Dick-Umans 2009' exists: Kevin Dick and Chris Umans, 'Improved inapproximability factors for some Sigma2p minimization problems', ECCC TR09-107. They give n^{1/3-eps} and n^{1/2-eps}, improving n^{1/4-eps}, plus a matching O(n^{1/2}) randomized approximation with an NP oracle for one problem. The agent's sampling-reduction argument is its own reasoning, as it says.

checks.citation: Russell Impagliazzo, Valentine Kabanets, Ilya Volkovich. The Power of Natural Properties as Oracles. CCC 2018. Also: Synergy Between Circuit Obfuscation and Circuit Minimization, APPROX/RANDOM 2023 (ECCC TR23-079). Related: Mazor-Pass CCC 2024.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search snippets. CCC 2018 (LIPIcs 102, 7:1-7:20; journal version Computational Complexity 32(2):6, 2023): assuming iO exists, SAT and MCSP are equivalent in that one has a ZPP algorithm iff the other does (Cor. 6: MCSP in ZPP iff NP = ZPP). APPROX/RANDOM 2023 (LIPIcs 275, 31:1-31:21; the ECCC TR23-079 title is 'Mutual Empowerment between Circuit Obfuscation and Circuit Minimization'): if computationally secure perfect iO exists, then MCSP in BPP iff NP = ZPP, and ZPEXP != BPP. If MCSP in BPP, statistical and computational security of iO are equivalent. The main tool is an MCSP-oracle universal distinguisher. The 'lexicographically smallest equivalent circuit in PH' point is only a footnote (the best-possible-obfuscator observation), not a theorem. Mazor-Pass: the exact title is 'Gap MCSP Is Not (Levin) NP-Complete in Obfustopia', CCC 2024, LIPIcs 300, art. 36; ePrint 2024/420; ECCC TR24-053. Under iO plus subexponentially secure OWFs, a gap version of MCSP is not NP-complete under randomized Levin reductions; a later ECCC revision says 'not NP-hard w.r.t. Levin reductions'. The 'non-black-box reduction' wording was not confirmed.

checks.citation: Yanyi Liu, Rafael Pass. On One-way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity. FOCS 2020; arXiv:2009.11514; IACR ePrint 2020/423. Related: Liu-Pass CCC 2022.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search snippets of the arXiv/ePrint abstracts (arxiv.org blocked). FOCS 2020; arXiv:2009.11514; ePrint 2020/423; ECCC TR20-052. Statement: for every polynomial t(n) >= (1+eps)n, OWFs exist iff K^t is mildly hard on average: there is a polynomial p such that no PPT algorithm computes K^t on more than a 1 - 1/p(n) fraction of uniform n-bit strings. The paper quantifies 'for every t' outside the equivalence; the agent's version puts it inside, which the paper implies. CCC 2022 (LIPIcs 234, 35:1-35:17; ECCC TR22-084): for all sufficiently large c, prBPP = prP iff every BPTIME(n^c) algorithm fails, for long enough z, on some x to decide whether Kt(x|z) >= n-1 or <= O(log n). Caveat on relevance: the hardness is average-case over uniform strings, not over trained-network truth tables.

checks.citation: Shuichi Hirahara, Rahul Ilango, Ryan Williams. Beating Brute Force for Compression Problems. STOC 2024, pp. 659-670; ECCC TR23-171. Related: Mazor-Pass ITCS 2024.
checks.corrected_finding: The paper, venue, pages and ECCC number are confirmed from search snippets. Every compression problem with decoder time t has non-uniform circuits of size 2^{4l/5} * poly(t(n)) that find a description of length l. This beats brute force O(2^l t(n)) when l >> log t(n). The construction adapts Fiat-Naor function inversion plus hashing. Correction for MCSP: the circuits have size 2^{(4/5)w + o(w)} * poly(2^n) with w = s(n) * log2(s(n)+n), not 2^{4s/5}. For K^t the size is 2^{(4/5)l} * poly(t). The paper also gives nontrivial circuits for K^t on average and for NP relations with compressible instance-witness pairs. Mazor-Pass, 'The Non-Uniform Perebor Conjecture for Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity is False' (ITCS 2024), is confirmed via the Computational Complexity blog (Nov 2023). The dspace.mit.edu URL was not openable here.

checks.citation: Leonid A. Levin. Universal Sequential Search Problems. Problems of Information Transmission 9(3):115-116 (English translation pp. 265-266), 1973.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search results: Probl. Peredachi Inf. 9(3):115-116 (1973); English: Problems Inform. Transmission 9(3):265-266; received 7 Jun 1972. The note's headline result is the universality (NP-completeness) of six search problems. The optimal-search statement in the 2^{l(p)} t_p form is a later restatement, as the agent said. arXiv:1702.03152 is Fouad B. Chedid, 'A Variation of Levin Search for All Well-Defined Problems' (2017); it restates Levin search time as about 2^{l(p*)} t*. Allender-Buhrman-Koucky-van Melkebeek-Ronneburger, 'Power from Random Strings', is confirmed: FOCS 2002 pp. 669-678; SICOMP 35(6):1467-1493, 2006. R_Kt is EXP-complete under P/poly truth-table reductions, and EXP = NP^{R_Kt}. Note that R_Kt is the set of strings with Kt(x) >= |x|/2, so 'its decision version is EXP-hard' should be read as that set.

checks.citation: Esty Kelman, Guy Kindler, Noam Lifshitz, Dor Minzer, Muli Safra. Towards a Proof of the Fourier-Entropy Conjecture? FOCS 2020; GAFA 2020. arXiv:1911.10579.
checks.corrected_finding: Confirmed from search snippets of the arXiv abstract (arxiv.org blocked). arXiv:1911.10579 (24 Nov 2019, rev. 7 May 2020); GAFA 30 (Dec 2020), DOI 10.1007/s00039-020-00544-2; also FOCS 2020. From the abstract: the Fourier spectrum of a constant-variance Boolean f is concentrated on 2^{O(I[f] log I[f])} characters, improving Friedgut. Functions with total influence <= K are agnostically learnable with membership queries in time 2^{O(K log K)}. Removing the log factor would essentially resolve the Fourier-entropy conjecture and Mansour's conjecture for DNF. The poly(n)-time claim for I = O(log n / log log n) is not in the abstract; it is the agent's derived corollary of the 2^{O(K log K)} bound, presumably with poly(n) factors and constant eps. The Friedgut 2^{O(I/eps)}-junta statement matches the standard theorem.

items.citation: Bazinet, M., Zantedeschi, V., Germain, P. 'Bound to Disagree: Generalization Bounds via Certifiable Surrogates.' UAI 2026 (PMLR 337:491-520 per search snippet; OpenReview CZeG5HW1Y5 per repo README). Numbers below were read this session from the notebook outputs in a local clone of the official repo GRAAL-Research/Bound-to-Disagree (result_plots/pactl_results.ipynb). The arXiv and PMLR pages could not be opened.
items.finding: Bound: err(f) <= cert(h) + binomial-tail upper bound on Pr[f != h], with the disagreement estimated on an unlabeled split independent of f and h (about 18% of the training data). The surrogate h is Lotfi-style subspace plus quantization (intrinsic_dim = 100) with a data-dependent prior (prior_size 0.2). MNIST CNN: f test error 0.50%, surrogate test error 0.89%, cert(h) 2.45%, disagreement bound 1.00%, total 3.45% (+/-0.11 over 5 seeds). CIFAR-10 ResNet18: f test error 5.84%, surrogate test error 14.95%, cert(h) 20.15%, disagreement bound 14.91%, total 35.06%. The repo's headline figure hard-codes the best results: 1.78% on MNIST (sample-compression surrogate) and 17.36% on CIFAR-10 (coreset surrogate). Norm-based baselines are 3.1e8 % and 3.8e21 %. A third-party review (pith.science, unconfirmed) flags the variant that distils on the available data as not valid as written.
items.relevance: This is the most direct published measurement of 'f is eps-close to a short g' on real data. MNIST: yes. A compressed surrogate with 100 subspace coordinates lies within about 1% of f. CIFAR-10: no, at this description length. The best compressed surrogate found disagrees with ResNet18 on about 15% of inputs, so the 2*eps term dominates. Caveat: the surrogate's code is relative to a prior trained on held-out data, so it is not a data-free K_eps.

items.citation: Lotfi, S., Finzi, M., Kapoor, S., Potapczynski, A., Goldblum, M., Wilson, A. G. 'PAC-Bayes Compression Bounds So Tight That They Can Explain Generalization.' NeurIPS 2022 (NeurIPS 35:31459-31473). UNVERIFIED as a web page: arxiv.org and proceedings.neurips.cc were blocked. The four data-independent bounds and the four transfer bounds were confirmed in a local clone of the authors' repo (notebooks/plot_fig1_transfer.py).
items.finding: Method: train in a random seeded subspace of dimension d (about 1e2 to 1e4), use quantization-aware training on a learned codebook, then arithmetic-code. Data-independent bounds (repo-confirmed): MNIST 11.6%, FashionMNIST 32.8%, CIFAR-10 58.2%, CIFAR-100 94.6%. With transfer priors (repo-confirmed): 9.0%, 28.2%, 35.1%, 81.3%. With data-dependent priors (snippet): MNIST 1.4%, CIFAR-10 16.6%, ImageNet 40.9% (93.5-94.1% data-independent; versions differ). Snippet, UNVERIFIED: the best MNIST code is 0.38 KB (KB = 8192 bits, so about 3,100 bits) for LeNet-5, against 6.23 KB for Zhou et al. Own arithmetic: 3,113 bits x ln2 / 60,000 = 0.036, so the complexity term is small and the 11.6% is mostly the compressed model's own training error plus the kl slack. Pruning plus quantization reportedly gives 47.9% on MNIST. The authors report that larger models compress further.
items.relevance: This gives an upper bound on K_eps for small vision nets, found by a polynomial-time heuristic search (subspace training) rather than exhaustive search. But the certified object is the compressed g trained inside the subspace, not an independently trained f. Its accuracy loss (tens of percent on CIFAR-10) shows that at about 1e3-1e4 bits a g matching a strong CIFAR f is not known.

items.citation: Zhou, W., Veitch, V., Austern, M., Adams, R. P., Orbanz, P. 'Non-vacuous Generalization Bounds at the ImageNet Scale: A PAC-Bayesian Compression Approach.' ICLR 2019. UNVERIFIED (snippets only). The ImageNet sizes were cross-checked against comments in the Lotfi repo file notebooks/replicate_imagenet_bound_error.py, opened locally.
items.finding: Pipeline: prune, quantize and code an off-the-shelf model, then add noise and apply a PAC-Bayes bound on compressed size. MNIST LeNet-5 at an effective 6.23 KiB (about 51,000 bits) gives a top-1 bound of about 46%. ImageNet MobileNet, 67% pruned, about 1.39M weights, 15 clusters: 452 KiB, effective 350 KiB (2,867,200 bits, per the repo comment), top-1 bound below 96.5%, top-5 below 89%. Nets trained on random labels compress less, which the authors frame as an absolute limit on expected compressibility as a function of generalization error.
items.relevance: This is a data point on how many bits off-the-shelf compression needs while keeping f's accuracy. Own arithmetic: 51,000 x ln2 / 60,000 = 0.59, so the code is short enough to be non-vacuous but far from tight. The random-label result is evidence that compressibility tracks generalization, which is the premise of the K_eps(f) bound.

items.citation: Han, S., Mao, H., Dally, W. J. 'Deep Compression: Compressing Deep Neural Networks with Pruning, Trained Quantization and Huffman Coding.' ICLR 2016. UNVERIFIED (search snippets of the arXiv tables).
items.finding: Compression without accuracy loss (eps about 0): LeNet-300-100 goes from 1070 KB to 27 KB (40x) at 1.58% error (reference 1.64%). LeNet-5 goes from 1720 KB to 44 KB (39x) at 0.74% error (reference 0.80%). About 8% of weights survive pruning, at about 5-6 bits per kept weight.
items.relevance: This calibrates K_eps at eps near 0. Own arithmetic: 27 KB is about 221k bits, giving bits x ln2 / m = 2.6 at m = 60k. 44 KB is about 360k bits, giving 4.2. Both are vacuous. Near-lossless descriptions of trained nets are about 100x longer than the about-3-kbit approximate descriptions above, so the eps-K tradeoff is steep: short descriptions exist only once some disagreement is allowed.

items.citation: Li, C., Farkhoor, H., Liu, R., Yosinski, J. 'Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes.' ICLR 2018. UNVERIFIED (snippets from the Uber blog, OpenReview and arXiv excerpts).
items.finding: d_int90 is the random-subspace dimension at which training reaches 90% of baseline performance. MNIST: about 750 for a fully connected net (about 0.4% of its parameters) and about 290 for LeNet (275 in one arXiv table). CIFAR-10: about 9k (FC) and about 2.9k (LeNet) in the ICLR version, 7.5k and 2.5k in an earlier draft.
items.relevance: This is the origin of the seeded-subspace code that Lotfi and Bazinet use. Note that d_int90 targets 90% of baseline accuracy, not agreement with a particular f, so it is a loose proxy for K_eps. A subspace net at d_int90 on MNIST (about 88-89% accuracy) is far from eps-close to a 99% f.

items.citation: Hsu, D., Ji, Z., Telgarsky, M., Wang, L. 'Generalization bounds via distillation.' ICLR 2021 (Spotlight). UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: The original f inherits the bound of its distilled g plus a distillation distance. The distance is measured on samples from an augmentation distribution with bounded density ratio to D_X, so it needs no fresh labels. The analysis covers conv, FC and skip connections. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR show f and its distillation generalize similarly. Per a snippet recorded in this project's literature.md: ResNet8, test error 0.067 on CIFAR-10 and 0.008 on MNIST. Distillation shrinks standard bounds by about 1e10, from about 1e15, so they remain above 1. That last point is inferred and not re-checked here.
items.relevance: This is the same f -> g -> bound reduction as the project's, with the closeness term certified on synthetic inputs. That makes it the closest analogue to the known-D_X case. The bounds stay numerically vacuous, so it does not by itself show that trained nets are eps-close to short g.

items.citation: Arora, S., Ge, R., Neyshabur, B., Zhang, Y. 'Stronger generalization bounds for deep nets via a compression approach.' ICML 2018 (PMLR 80). UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: Layer-wise noise stability (noise injected at lower layers is attenuated) lets each layer be compressed by randomized linear-algebraic projection, with a helper string of random bits. The compressed parameter count enters the bound. Experiments: VGG-19 on CIFAR-10 (100% train, 92.45% val accuracy). Their bounds are orders of magnitude better than norm-based bounds, but this project's literature notes record them as still vacuous (about 1e5). Exact effective-parameter counts were not retrieved.
items.relevance: This is an efficient (polynomial-time) construction of g from f by a sampling-type argument, the closest classical relative of the proposed neuron or weight subsampling. Its bound covers g, not f, and the compressed size it reaches for VGG-19 is too large to certify CIFAR-10 nets.

items.citation: Stanton, S., Izmailov, P., Kirichenko, P., Alemi, A. A., Wilson, A. G. 'Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?' NeurIPS 2021. UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: Fidelity (top-1 agreement between student and teacher) is often low even when the student has capacity to match. On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-56 students, the best agreement reported is around 85% (approximate, setting not pinned down from snippets), 'nowhere near 99%'. On EMNIST, with enough distillation data, agreement exceeds 99%. The authors identify optimization difficulty as the main cause.
items.relevance: This bears directly on 'is f close to a small g in practice, and can SGD find it?'. On easy data, distillation finds g within about 1% of f. On harder data, ordinary distillation leaves eps of about 15%, which would swamp a K_eps bound. It also shows that the search, not just existence, is the bottleneck: even same-capacity students fail to match.

items.citation: Ba, L. J., Caruana, R. 'Do Deep Nets Really Need to be Deep?' NIPS 2014. UNVERIFIED (snippets only). Follow-up: Urban et al., 'Do Deep Convolutional Nets Really Need to be Deep and Convolutional?', ICLR 2017 (arXiv 1603.05691), also UNVERIFIED.
items.finding: Shallow mimic nets match deep nets on TIMIT. On CIFAR-10, the shallow student needed a conv layer and about 30x the teacher's parameters and still trailed the teacher by several points. Urban et al. find that students need multiple conv layers to match deep conv teachers.
items.relevance: This is evidence that on CIFAR-scale tasks, eps-close surrogates from a restricted (shallow) family are not shorter than f. Shortness must come from quantization or low-dimensional codes within a similar architecture, not from a simpler architecture.

items.citation: Nakkiran, P., Kaplun, G., Kalimeris, D., Yang, T., Edelman, B. L., Zhang, F., Barak, B. 'SGD on Neural Networks Learns Functions of Increasing Complexity.' NeurIPS 2019. UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: Using a conditional-mutual-information measure of how much one classifier explains another, almost all of the early performance gain of SGD is explained by a linear classifier. This holds on CIFAR, MNIST, MLPs and CNNs. That linear classifier is retained through training to zero training error. Later training adds increasingly complex functions (stated as a conjecture). Exact CIFAR-10 fractions were not retrieved.
items.relevance: This supports a hierarchical picture: f is close to a very short g (linear) on the inputs that g already gets right, and the residual is where the complexity lives. It suggests a staged search for g (linear, then low-complexity corrections) rather than exhaustive search.

items.citation: Valle-Perez, G., Camargo, C. Q., Louis, A. A. 'Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions.' ICLR 2019. UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: For small Boolean nets (n = 7 inputs), the probability P(f) that random parameters implement function f spans many orders of magnitude and is exponentially biased toward low (Lempel-Ziv) complexity, consistent with the AIT bound P(f) <~ 2^(-a K(f) - b). The authors give PAC-Bayes bounds via a Gaussian-process approximation of P(U) for FC and CNN nets on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
items.relevance: This is the strongest evidence for the uniform-Boolean-input case: functions reached by random or trained nets are typically exactly or nearly simple. The certified object, though, is the Bayesian posterior via a GP approximation, and the evidence is at n = 7. It does not show eps-closeness of SGD-trained f to short circuits at n = 20-50.

items.citation: Mingard, C., Valle-Perez, G., Skalse, J., Louis, A. A. 'Is SGD a Bayesian sampler? Well, almost.' JMLR 22(79):1-64, 2021. Also Mingard, C., Rees, H., Valle-Perez, G., Louis, A. A. 'Deep neural networks have an inbuilt Occam's razor.' Nature Communications 16, 2025 (arXiv 2304.06670). Both UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: JMLR: P_SGD(f|S) correlates remarkably well with the Bayesian posterior P_B(f|S), which is strongly biased toward low-error, low-complexity functions. The inductive bias sits mainly in the parameter-function map, not in SGD. Nat. Commun.: for fully connected nets on Boolean functions, an exponential preference for Kolmogorov-simple functions counteracts the exponential growth in the number of complex functions. The published referee file criticizes the setting (7 inputs, 10 layers) as unrealistic.
items.relevance: This supports the premise that SGD-trained f sits near short-description functions, at least for small Boolean tasks with uniform inputs. It gives no algorithm for finding the short g and no eps-K numbers at realistic sizes.

items.citation: Shah, H., Tamuly, K., Raghunathan, A., Jain, P., Netrapalli, P. 'The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks.' NeurIPS 2020. UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: On synthetic piecewise-linear and image datasets with features of controlled simplicity, SGD-trained nets can rely exclusively on the simplest predictive feature and ignore more complex but also predictive features. This extreme simplicity bias can hurt in-distribution generalization and robustness, and ensembles and adversarial training do not mitigate it.
items.relevance: This is evidence that trained f is often functionally close to a function of one simple feature (for example a linear threshold), which favors short surrogates. It also cautions that the relevant notion of 'simple' is architecture-induced (linear or low-frequency features), so the surrogate family searched should match it.

items.citation: Huh, M., Mobahi, H., Zhang, R., Cheung, B., Agrawal, P., Isola, P. 'The Low-Rank Simplicity Bias in Deep Networks.' TMLR 2023 (arXiv 2021). UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: Deeper networks are biased toward solutions with low effective rank of the embedding Gram matrix, both at initialization and after training, robustly across hyperparameters. For deep linear nets, the volume fraction of low effective-rank solutions grows monotonically with depth (proved asymptotically). Linear over-parameterization of standard nets at training time improves generalization, including on ImageNet.
items.relevance: This gives a concrete structural handle for short g: low-rank factorization of layers. Low-rank structure is also what makes neuron or weight subsampling and rank truncation good compressors with small Pr[f != g].

items.citation: Smallest MNIST models, NOT peer-reviewed: GitHub ruslangrimov/mnist-minimal-model ('minimal model that can achieve 99% accuracy'); GitHub aknakshay/MNIST-Challenge; Medium post by D. Mitra, 'Getting to 99.4% accuracy in less than 8000 parameters'. All UNVERIFIED (snippets only).
items.finding: Reported: 99.4% with 7,940 parameters (Medium). 99.2% with 8,640 parameters (standard conv) and 98.42% with 4,967 parameters (separable conv) (aknakshay). The ruslangrimov record holder uses 3x3 conv (8 filters), then separable convs, then global average pooling, but its parameter count was not visible. A linear classifier (7,850 parameters) gets about 92%. Stated widely, not re-checked: LeNet-5 (about 60k parameters) reaches about 99.0-99.2%.
items.relevance: This is a floor on architecture size for 98-99% MNIST accuracy: a few thousand parameters. Own arithmetic: 8,640 parameters at 8 bits is about 69k bits, giving bits x ln2 / m = 0.80 at m = 60k; at 4 bits it gives 0.40. So a from-scratch tiny net is not short enough. The about-3-kbit Lotfi codes depend on seeded subspaces, which spend about 100 coordinates rather than thousands of free parameters.

report.synthesis:
Access caveat: WebFetch could not reach arxiv.org or proceedings.neurips.cc; the environment's network policy blocks them. No paper page was opened in this session. To change that, add those hosts under Allowed domains in the cloud environment's Network access settings. Each item comes from search-result snippets plus, for two papers, local clones of the official code repos made by an earlier sweep. Bazinet et al.: all numbers were read from notebook outputs this session. Lotfi et al.: the four data-independent and four transfer bound values are in the repo. Everything else is UNVERIFIED. The 'own arithmetic' figures are mine.

Is a trained f close to a function with a short description, and how short?

(1) MNIST: yes, at a few kbit with about 1% disagreement. Bazinet et al.'s repo shows an MNIST CNN (0.50% test error) within a certified 1.00% disagreement of a 100-dimensional subspace-quantized surrogate, giving a total bound of 3.45%. Lotfi et al. compress MNIST nets to about 0.38 KB, about 3,100 bits (snippet), so K ln2/m is about 0.036. Caveat: Bazinet's surrogate code is relative to a data-dependent prior.

(2) The eps-K tradeoff is steep. Near-lossless codes are about 100x longer. Deep Compression keeps accuracy at 27-44 KB, about 2-4e5 bits, which is vacuous (bits x ln2/m = 2.6-4.2). Zhou et al. need about 51 kbit for LeNet-5, giving a bound of about 46%. Tiny 99%-accurate MNIST architectures still need about 5-9k parameters, about 0.4-0.8 in the Occam term at 4-8 bits.

(3) CIFAR-10 and harder data: not shown at any known description length. Bazinet's best compressed surrogate for ResNet18 (5.84% error) disagrees about 14.9% of the time. Lotfi's data-independent bound is 58.2%. Distillation reaches only about 85% top-1 agreement on CIFAR-100 versus over 99% on EMNIST (Stanton et al.). Shallow mimics on CIFAR-10 need 30x the parameters (Ba & Caruana).

(4) Simplicity-bias studies (Valle-Perez et al. 2019; Mingard et al. 2021, 2025) make the premise plausible for uniform Boolean inputs: the function prior and SGD's posterior are exponentially biased toward low-complexity functions. But the evidence is at n = 7, or rests on GP approximations of the Bayesian posterior, and gives no eps-closeness numbers for SGD nets at realistic n. Nakkiran et al. (a linear classifier explains early SGD and is retained), Shah et al. (extreme reliance on the simplest feature) and Huh et al. (low effective rank) suggest f is partly a short function plus a complex residual, so eps-closeness depends on how much the residual matters.

For the compute question: every K_eps upper bound in the literature was found by a polynomial-time heuristic, not by search. The heuristics are seeded-subspace training (Li et al. 2018; Lotfi et al.), prune-quantize-code (Han et al.; Zhou et al.), randomized layer projection under noise stability (Arora et al.), and distillation (Hsu et al.; Bazinet et al.). The empirical gap between these heuristics and the true K_eps is unknown. Stanton et al.'s finding that same-capacity students fail to match teachers because of optimization suggests the search, not existence, is the binding constraint on hard data. Neuron or weight subsampling is closest in spirit to Arora et al.'s randomized compression, and low-rank or simplicity bias is the structure that would make it work. None of these papers reports Maurey-style neuron subsampling of a trained net as a certificate with measured Pr[f != g]; that looks like an open, testable gap.

items.citation: Matti Kääriäinen. 'Generalization Error Bounds Using Unlabeled Data.' COLT 2005 (LNCS 3559), pp. 127-142. DOI 10.1007/11503415_9.
items.finding: The paper gives two semi-supervised bounds, both built on estimating with unlabeled data how often a pair of classifiers disagrees. Method 1 covers only the realizable case. Method 2 uses unlabeled data to turn a bound for a randomized classifier into a bound for a deterministic one. The worked example is a cross-validation bound. The randomized classifier is uniform over the k classifiers from the CV rounds, and each one is certified on its own held-out fold. The result is 'a semi-supervised bound for classifiers learned based on all the labeled data', and SVM experiments on MNIST suggest it 'may be tight enough to be useful in practice'. The mechanism is presumably err(f) <= err(Gibbs over CV classifiers) + E_h Pr_x[f(x) != h(x)], with the second term estimated on unlabeled data. I did not see that exact statement or its constants in any text I could reach.
items.relevance: This is the closest prior work, and it is essentially the twin bound with k twins instead of one half-data twin. It gives a rigorous bound on the full-data model f. It needs unlabeled samples from D_X (with D_X known, sampling is free) and makes no stability assumption. The only difference from our twin bound is k-fold Gibbs twins instead of a single f_half. Averaging the k fold classifiers makes the test-set term tighter. The twin bound itself should therefore not be claimed as new.

items.citation: Matti Kääriäinen and John Langford. 'A Comparison of Tight Generalization Error Bounds.' ICML 2005. Companion paper: M. Kääriäinen, 'Semi-Supervised Model Selection Based on Cross-Validation', IJCNN 2006, pp. 1894-1899 (earlier version: ICSI TR-05-010).
items.finding: The ICML paper compares tight true-error bounds empirically. Its tools include 'a technique using unlabeled data for a tight derandomization of randomized bounds', a tight progressive-validation bound and the exact (binomial) test-set bound, all implemented in the 'semibound' package. The IJCNN 2006 paper applies structural risk minimization to the CV-based semi-supervised bound to choose SVM parameters. The chosen models have 'roughly the same accuracy' as plain CV selection, and the method also gives 'a reliable and reasonably tight generalization error guarantee for the chosen classifier'.
items.relevance: This shows the CV-twin plus unlabeled-disagreement bound was implemented and found usable for SVMs in 2005-2006. I found no application to deep networks. The exact binomial test-set bound is the right way to certify err(f_half) on the held-out half.

items.citation: Omid Madani, David M. Pennock, Gary W. Flake. 'Co-Validation: Using Model Disagreement on Unlabeled Data to Validate Classification Algorithms.' NIPS 17 (2004), pp. 873-880.
items.finding: The paper measures how often two independently trained classifiers disagree on unlabeled data. It shows that this disagreement gives a lower bound on prediction (generalization) error and a tight upper bound on the 'variance of prediction error'. It uses this for model selection and finds it most useful in active learning, where cross-validation overestimates error.
items.relevance: It rests on the same triangle inequality for the disagreement pseudo-metric, used in the other direction: disagreement <= err(h1) + err(h2) gives a lower bound on error. That direction does not bound f's error from above. It does show that a twin's disagreement term is at most err(f) + err(f_half), so the twin bound is at most err(f) + 2 err(f_half).

items.citation: Dale Schuurmans. 'A New Metric-Based Approach to Model Selection.' AAAI 1997. Extended in D. Schuurmans and F. Southey, 'Metric-Based Methods for Adaptive Model Selection and Regularization', Machine Learning 48 (2002).
items.finding: The method builds a metric on hypotheses from their predictions on unlabeled data, d(f,g) = Pr_x[f != g] (or the L2 analogue). It uses the triangle inequality d(f,target) <= d(f,h) + d(h,target) to detect when empirical error estimates cannot be trusted. Its only extra requirement is an auxiliary unlabeled sample. It reportedly 'dramatically outperform[s]' earlier model selection methods on polynomial curve fitting. Bengio and Chapados (JMLR 2003) credit it with introducing metric-based model selection through triangle-inequality violations.
items.relevance: This is the origin of the 'unlabeled data gives a metric, then apply the triangle inequality' ingredient in the twin bound. It is used heuristically for model selection and gives no certified bound on a full-data model.

items.citation: Preetum Nakkiran and Yamini Bansal. 'Distributional Generalization: A New Kind of Generalization.' arXiv:2009.08092, 2020 (preprint; I found no peer-reviewed venue).
items.finding: It states an 'Agreement Property'. For classifiers f and g trained on independent samples, test accuracy of f is approximately E[Pr_x(f(x) = g(x))]. Equivalently, the disagreement rate is close to the test error, not just correlated with it. This was observed across neural nets, kernel SVMs and decision trees. It is an empirical conjecture that holds in expectation, not for each pair.
items.relevance: This is not a bound. It does predict how tight the twin bound will be. If f_half and f behave like independently trained models, Pr[f != f_half] is about err, so the twin bound is about err(f_half) + err(f), roughly twice the true error. Sharing data (S_1 is a subset of S) should lower the disagreement, but nobody seems to have measured this for the nested full-versus-half pair.

items.citation: Yiding Jiang, Vaishnavh Nagarajan, Christina Baek, J. Zico Kolter. 'Assessing Generalization of SGD via Disagreement.' ICLR 2022 (spotlight). Critique: Andreas Kirsch and Yarin Gal, 'A Note on "Assessing Generalization of SGD via Disagreement"', TMLR 2022 (arXiv:2202.01851).
items.finding: Two SGD runs on the same training set, differing only in seed, disagree on unlabeled test inputs at about their test error. They name this the Generalization Disagreement Equality (GDE). Points fall within y = (1 +/- 0.1)x when the two runs use different data or differ in everything, and within (1 +/- 0.3)x when only initialization or data order differs. Experiments cover ResNets on CIFAR-10/100 and SVHN. The theory proves GDE in expectation over training randomness, assuming the ensemble is class-wise calibrated. Kirsch and Gal show the same holds for any discriminative model, with |test error - disagreement| bounded by the class-aggregated calibration error (equivalent to ACE/SCE). They note that measuring calibration needs labels and that calibration gets worse exactly as disagreement grows.
items.relevance: This is an estimator, not a rigorous bound on f. It needs a calibration assumption that cannot be checked without labels, and it holds in expectation, not for a given pair. It is the strongest evidence that the twin's disagreement term is about the size of err(f), so the twin bound typically loses about a factor of 2. Unlike GDE, the twin bound needs no calibration. It pays for that with the extra err(f_half).

items.citation: Christina Baek, Yiding Jiang, Aditi Raghunathan, J. Zico Kolter. 'Agreement-on-the-Line: Predicting the Performance of Neural Networks under Distribution Shift.' NeurIPS 2022.
items.finding: Wherever accuracy-on-the-line holds, agreement between pairs of neural networks out of distribution is linearly related to their agreement in distribution. The slope and bias match the accuracy line. Out-of-distribution accuracy can then be predicted from unlabeled OOD data, with mean absolute error of 2% or less on benchmarks where the phenomenon holds. It beats ATC, DOC-Feat and average confidence. It appears to hold only for neural networks.
items.relevance: This is an estimator, not a bound. It needs many trained models, labeled in-distribution data and unlabeled shifted data. In our setting D_X is known and there is no shift, so the disagreement term can be certified directly by sampling and no linear fit is needed.

items.citation: Saurabh Garg, Sivaraman Balakrishnan, J. Zico Kolter, Zachary C. Lipton. 'RATT: Leveraging Unlabeled Data to Guarantee Generalization.' ICML 2021 (PMLR 139:3598-3609, long talk).
items.finding: RATT adds unlabeled points with random labels to the training set, trains as usual, and tracks error on the random-label portion. Low error on clean data plus high error on the random data certifies low true risk, up to an O(1/sqrt(m)) term. The proof covers 0-1 empirical risk minimization and linear classifiers trained by gradient descent. For binary labels it works because a lower bound on population error on mislabeled points upper-bounds error on the true distribution. As I recall it, the bound contains a '1 - 2 x error on mislabeled' term; I could not check this. The bound is non-vacuous for MLPs and ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and the direct bound is vacuous on CIFAR-100.
items.relevance: This bounds the model actually trained on all labeled data without a validation set, but it changes how f is trained, since f must also fit the random-label points. Its guarantee for deep nets rests on assumptions the theorem does not cover (it is proven only for ERM and linear GD). The twin bound leaves f's training untouched and is rigorous for any learner. It costs a second training run plus the disagreement term.

items.citation: Michael Kearns and Dana Ron. 'Algorithmic Stability and Sanity-Check Bounds for Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation.' Neural Computation 11(6):1427-1453, 1999 (COLT 1997 version).
items.finding: These are 'sanity-check' bounds. The leave-one-out estimate of the full-data hypothesis's error is never much worse than the training-error estimate, which gives VC-type rates under a new and weaker notion called error stability. They show some form of algorithmic stability is necessary for any nontrivial leave-one-out bound. For training-error minimization, worst-case bounds must still depend on the VC dimension.
items.relevance: It bounds the full-data f only under a stability assumption that must be proven a priori. For SGD-trained networks that assumption cannot be checked and VC-type rates are vacuous. The twin bound replaces assumed stability with stability that is measured and certified: Pr_{D_X}[f != f_half] is a data-dependent hypothesis-stability term.

items.citation: Avrim Blum, Adam Kalai, John Langford. 'Beating the Hold-Out: Bounds for K-Fold and Progressive Cross-Validation.' COLT 1999, pp. 203-208. DOI 10.1145/307400.307439.
items.finding: To avoid the dependencies behind sanity-check bounds, they analyze a k-fold hypothesis that is a randomized combination (or average) of the k fold hypotheses. For algorithms insensitive to example order, the k-fold error estimate has no larger moments than a hold-out of size m/k, and is strictly better for 2 < k < n. They also introduce progressive validation, which is about as good as a hold-out while training on more examples on average.
items.relevance: This is rigorous, but for the randomized fold classifier, not for f trained on all the data. Kääriäinen's unlabeled-data derandomization is what carries this guarantee over to f. Combining the two is the k-twin version of our bound.

items.citation: Olivier Bousquet and André Elisseeff. 'Stability and Generalization.' JMLR 2:499-526, 2002.
items.finding: It introduces uniform stability (and related notions) and proves exponential generalization bounds for any uniformly stable algorithm with bounded loss, applied to RKHS/Tikhonov and KL regularization and to SVM regression and classification. I recall the usual rate beta = O(1/(lambda m)) for regularized methods, but I could not confirm the exact constants.
items.relevance: It gives rigorous bounds on the full-data model, but stability must be proven for the algorithm in advance. For the 0-1 error of classifiers it is usually available only through margin or real-valued surrogates. The twin bound needs no a priori stability.

items.citation: Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht, Yoram Singer. 'Train Faster, Generalize Better: Stability of Stochastic Gradient Descent.' ICML 2016 (PMLR 48:1225-1234).
items.finding: SGD is uniformly stable in the Bousquet-Elisseeff sense. For convex, Lipschitz, smooth losses, stability is roughly (sum of step sizes)/n. In the strongly convex case it stays stable however long training runs. In the nonconvex smooth case the number of steps can grow as n^c for a small c > 1 with stability still vanishing. Dropout improves all the bounds.
items.relevance: It gives rigorous expected-generalization bounds on the trained model, but only under Lipschitz and smoothness constants for the surrogate loss. These are typically vacuous for practical deep nets and do not bound 0-1 error directly. The twin bound measures how far f is from a half-data retrain instead of bounding sensitivity in the worst case.

items.citation: Stephen Bates, Trevor Hastie, Robert Tibshirani. 'Cross-Validation: What Does It Estimate and How Well Does It Do It?' JASA 119(546):1434-1445, 2024 (arXiv:2104.00673).
items.finding: Cross-validation does not estimate the error of the model fit on the data at hand. For OLS it targets the average error over other training sets from the same population, and the same holds for data splitting, the bootstrap and Mallows' Cp. Naive CV confidence intervals can cover far below the nominal level because fold errors are correlated. Nested CV fixes coverage. With simple data splitting, refitting on the combined data invalidates the interval.
items.relevance: This is a modern statistical confirmation that CV, or holdout followed by refitting, does not certify the specific full-data f. That gap is exactly what the disagreement term Pr[f != f_half] pays for.

items.citation: Srinadh Bhojanapalli, Kimberly Wilber, Andreas Veit, Ankit Singh Rawat, Seungyeon Kim, Aditya Menon, Sanjiv Kumar. 'On the Reproducibility of Neural Network Predictions.' arXiv:2102.03349, 2021. Related: Q. Cormier, M. Milani Fard, K. Canini, M. R. Gupta, 'Launch and Iterate: Reducing Prediction Churn', NIPS 2016.
items.finding: Churn is the disagreement between identically configured retrains caused by initialization, mini-batch order and augmentation. It appears on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, SVHN and iNaturalist. Minimum-entropy regularization and co-distillation reduce it. On CIFAR-10, entropy regularization gives 94.05% accuracy and 5.59% churn, and co-distillation gives 94.25-94.63% accuracy and 5.14-4.29% churn. The baseline row was not visible in the snippet I saw. Milani Fard et al. regularize a new model toward the previous one with an MCMC stabilization operator, reducing churn without losing accuracy.
items.relevance: Even with identical data, retrain disagreement (about 4-6%) is close to the error rate (about 6%), so the twin's disagreement term is about the size of err(f). Churn reduction can shrink it, but only some forms keep the bound valid. Pulling f toward f_half (the Milani Fard approach) is fine, because f may depend on anything. Distilling f_half toward f would leak held-out labels from S_2 into f_half and invalidate the test-set bound on f_half.

items.relevance: This supports treating Pr_{D_X}[f != twin] as a stable, well-concentrated quantity, and so the twin bound's value as reproducible across seeds. report.synthesis:
Access caveat: none of these URLs could be opened. The session's network policy refused arxiv.org, openreview.net and proceedings.mlr.press, both through WebFetch and through curl (proxy 403 / DNS not resolved). Every item is therefore marked unverified. Existence, authors, venues and the quoted claims were checked only through web-search result summaries, which quote the abstracts and sometimes tables. Treat numbers that come only from snippets (the RATT formula shape, the Bousquet-Elisseeff rate, the churn table) as needing a check before citing. To verify against primary sources, arxiv.org and openreview.net need to be added under Allowed domains in the environment's network settings.

1. The twin bound is not new. err(f) <= err(f_half) + Pr[f != f_half] is the triangle inequality for the disagreement pseudo-metric, which Schuurmans (AAAI 1997) used heuristically for model selection. As a rigorous bound on the full-data classifier it appears in Kääriäinen (COLT 2005). There the twin is a Gibbs classifier over the k cross-validation fold classifiers, each certified on its held-out fold. Unlabeled data then derandomizes the bound to the classifier trained on all labels. The method was implemented in the 'semibound' package (Kääriäinen & Langford, ICML 2005) and used for SVM model selection with 'reasonably tight' guarantees (Kääriäinen, IJCNN 2006). Our version (one half-data twin, known D_X so the disagreement is certified by free sampling, deep networks) is a special case. The k-fold Gibbs twin is the stronger form. I found no paper applying it to modern deep networks, so an empirical study there would be new.

2. Rigour and requirements. The twin/Kääriäinen bound is rigorous for any learner with no stability assumption. It needs two things. First, f_half must be statistically independent of the held-out labels S_2, so it can be certified with an exact binomial test-set bound. Second, there must be unlabeled samples from D_X, or a known D_X, to certify the disagreement term; combine the two confidence levels with a union bound. f itself may depend on all of S arbitrarily. The other approaches compare as follows:
- CV and stability bounds (Kearns & Ron 1999; Bousquet & Elisseeff 2002; Hardt, Recht & Singer 2016) bound the full-data f only under a stability assumption proven in advance. That is unverifiable or vacuous for practical deep nets, and some stability is provably necessary for leave-one-out bounds.
- Blum, Kalai & Langford (1999) are rigorous, but for the randomized or averaged fold classifier, not for f.
- Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani (2024) show that CV estimates average error over training sets, not err(f).
- RATT (Garg et al. 2021) bounds f without validation data, but f must be trained with extra randomly labeled points, and it is proven only for ERM and linear GD.
- Disagreement estimators (Nakkiran & Bansal 2020; Jiang et al. 2022; Baek et al. 2022) are not bounds. They are equalities in expectation that rest on a calibration assumption, and Kirsch & Gal show the gap is bounded by a calibration error that needs labels to measure.
In short, the twin bound swaps assumed stability for stability that is measured on D_X and certified.

3. Expected tightness: about twice the error. GDE and the churn measurements (about 4-6% retrain disagreement for about 94%-accurate CIFAR-10 networks; disagreement within (1 +/- 0.1)x of test error across different data) suggest Pr[f != f_half] is about err. The twin bound would then be about err(f_half) + err(f), roughly 2x err. Madani et al.'s direction of the triangle inequality caps it at err(f) + 2 err(f_half). The f versus f_half pair is nested (S_1 is a subset of S), which should lower the disagreement below the independent-retrain level. I found no measurement of this nested pair, so that is something we should measure.

4. Shrinking the disagreement term without breaking validity (my own reasoning, not taken from these papers). Because only f_half has to be independent of S_2, coupling should run from the twin to f, never the other way. Options that keep the bound valid:
- train f_half on S_1 first, then get f by warm-start fine-tuning on all of S;
- regularize f toward f_half on unlabeled or D_X inputs (the stabilization operator of Milani Fard et al. 2016);
- use a shared seed and data order.
Co-distillation, or distilling f_half toward f, leaks S_2's labels into f_half and invalidates the bound.

5. Link to the compression programme. Both bounds have the form err(g) + Pr[f != g]. The compression bound certifies err(g) through an Occam/description-length term. The twin bound certifies it by holdout independence, at zero description cost but with a disagreement of about err. A hybrid is natural: pick a g trained on S_1, then compress it or search near it. That g gets both the holdout certificate and a small disagreement with f. Kääriäinen's k-fold Gibbs averaging is the obvious way to tighten the test-set term.

checks.corrected_finding: UNVERIFIED THIS PASS: papers.neurips.cc was unreachable and the search budget was used up. From memory of the abstract, the finding is accurate. Disagreement is how often two independently trained models disagree on unlabeled data. Per-instance disagreement is an unbiased estimate of the variance of error for that instance. Disagreement gives a lower bound on prediction (generalization) error and a tight upper bound on the 'variance of prediction error', taken across training sets. The method is especially effective in active learning, where cross-validation overestimates error. The pages 873-880 are not checked. The relevance inequality is correct: Pr[f != f_half] <= err(f) + err(f_half), so the twin bound is at most err(f) + 2 err(f_half) before estimation slack.

items.citation: Mathieu Bazinet, Valentina Zantedeschi, Pascal Germain. "Bound to Disagree: Generalization Bounds via Certifiable Surrogates." UAI 2026 (PMLR vol. 337); arXiv:2602.23128 (Feb 2026). The arXiv abstract page https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23128 could not be opened because arxiv.org is blocked here. I opened the authors' official code README instead.
items.finding: OPENED (README): confirms the title, the authors and UAI 2026. The experiments build certified surrogates of a fixed target network in six ways: (i) Pick-To-Learn, i.e. sample compression; (ii) coresets via the DeepCore library, i.e. a surrogate retrained on a selected subset of the training data; (iii) model compression via PACTL (Lotfi et al. 2022); (iv) PAC-Bayes via PBB (Perez-Ortiz et al. 2021); (v) quantization; (vi) model distillation. One dataset is Amazon polarity. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS of the arXiv abstract and HTML (details UNVERIFIED): the target's risk is bounded by the surrogate's certified risk plus a bound on the true target-surrogate disagreement, and that disagreement is estimated on an unlabeled set. The target model and its training are left unchanged. Experiments use MNIST, CIFAR10 and Amazon polarity. The paper says that 'a coreset can be viewed as the compression set' in its sample-compression theorem. The authors note that the bound is only as good as the surrogate's own certificate. They also note that the tightest bounds came WITHOUT minimizing disagreement on the unlabeled set. A separate result covers the case where disagreement is optimized on the data (distillation). A third-party review (pith.science) describes Theorem 4 as bounding the risk gap by an inverted binomial tail of the empirical disagreement. The same review says the unlabeled set must be independent of the target's training data. It also questions a uniform-over-h step in the distillation experiments. I could not get the bound values from the tables: the snippets show Random Coreset, Best Coreset and P2L rows for MNIST and CIFAR10, but garbled.
items.relevance: Closest prior art. This is the project's decomposition err(f) <= Bound(g) + Pr[f != g], already published. It includes the exact case the project asks about: a surrogate obtained by retraining on a small subset (coreset or P2L), certified by sample compression, plus disagreement certified on unlabeled data. The project must cite it and compare against it. Their finding that minimizing disagreement did not give the tightest bounds suggests the surrogate's own certificate dominates the total.

items.citation: Mathieu Bazinet, Valentina Zantedeschi, Pascal Germain. "Sample Compression Unleashed: New Generalization Bounds for Real Valued Losses." AISTATS 2025; arXiv:2409.17932. The arXiv page is blocked. I opened the official code README.
items.finding: OPENED (README): confirms the authors, AISTATS 2025 (OpenReview id 0ynSy2dwNi), and experiments on MNIST with P2L, PBB and regression forests. Erratum dated 16 Dec 2025: a bug in the P2L-bound code made the paper's P2L bounds slightly tighter than they should be. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS (UNVERIFIED): the paper extends sample-compression bounds from the 0-1 loss to real-valued losses. It also covers the non-consistent case, where the reconstructed predictor may err outside the compression set. The bounds do not depend on the number of parameters. CNNs are trained with P2L on binary MNIST pairs (e.g. MNIST08), and random forests are also tested. A footnote example uses m = 10,597, compression set size k = 92 and delta = 0.01. One snippet suggests a P2L bound of 1.42 against about 6.5 for the kl/binomial bounds on MNIST08, but the units and setup are unclear. Treat that number as UNVERIFIED.
items.relevance: Shows the scale of compression sets that greedy subset retraining reaches for CNNs on easy binary tasks: about 100 points out of about 10^4. That costs about k*log2(e*m/k) = 92*8.3, or roughly 760 bits, for the subset indices. This is a practical, polynomial-compute way to get a short description of a network-like g, and it is non-vacuous only when k << m. The non-consistent version allows a surrogate g that is not perfectly fit.

items.citation: Dario Paccagnan, Marco C. Campi, Simone Garatti. "The Pick-to-Learn Algorithm: Empowering Compression for Tight Generalization Bounds and Improved Post-training Performance." NeurIPS 2023 (spotlight). UNVERIFIED: the proceedings page could not be opened.
items.finding: UNVERIFIED (search snippets of the abstract and slides): P2L wraps any learning algorithm in a meta-algorithm that makes it a compression scheme, so the Campi-Garatti compression bounds apply to the output. On binary MNIST classification and on a synthetic regression task, the bounds are comparable or superior to test-set and PAC-Bayes bounds. The post-training performance is also better, because no data is held out. From my background knowledge, not checked against the text: P2L starts from an empty set, trains, adds the not-yet-selected example with the worst loss under the current model, and retrains. It stops when every remaining example meets the criterion. The output therefore depends only on the selected subset.
items.relevance: This is the concrete efficient search procedure for 'a small training subset that reproduces a trained-network-like predictor'. It needs k retrainings, or warm-started updates, instead of exponential enumeration. To reproduce a given f rather than the labels, one could run P2L using f's labels: they equal the true labels where f interpolates.

The size of the compressed set is a consistent estimator of the probability of change of compression. Under preference alone, no lower bounds are possible.

A fixed-size scheme implies PAC learnability. Maximum classes of VC dimension d have size-d schemes. Whether O(d)-size schemes always exist is still open. Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every class of VC dimension d has a scheme of size exp(O(d)). That does not settle the O(d) conjecture, which remains open. From my background knowledge, the standard form: a consistent size-k scheme gives err <= (k ln(e*m/k) + ln(1/delta)) / (m - k) with probability 1 - delta.
items.relevance: Sample compression is an Occam bound with a data-dependent codebook of log C(m,k), about k log(e*m/k), bits. For CIFAR-10 (m = 50,000), that term is at most 0.1 only when k is about 1,000 (2% of the data). The worst-case theory (exp(d), where d is on the order of the parameter count) says nothing useful for neural networks, so feasibility is entirely an empirical, data-dependent question.
