Pruning HALF of CIFAR-10 by EL2N slightly improves test accuracy. Up to 25% of CIFAR-100 can be pruned without loss. Erratum in v2: a Flax bug invalidated the GraNd-at-initialization results.

Data pruning for accuracy is therefore far from the compression needed for a bound, and matching accuracy is not the same as agreeing with f pointwise. The scores themselves are cheap selection heuristics that could seed a P2L-style search.

items.citation: Ben Sorscher, Robert Geirhos, Shashank Shekhar, Surya Ganguli, Ari S. Morcos. "Beyond Neural Scaling Laws: Beating Power Law Scaling via Data Pruning." NeurIPS 2022 (Outstanding Paper Award); arXiv:2206.14486. The arXiv page is blocked. I opened the authors' metric-scores README.
items.finding: OPENED (README): confirms the authors, NeurIPS 2022 and the Outstanding Paper Award. Lists the ImageNet pruning metrics benchmarked: self-supervised and supervised prototypes, DDD, EL2N (1 or 20 models), forgetting, influence-max, influence-sum-abs, active learning (the active-learning method keeps 80% of ImageNet), and random baselines. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS (UNVERIFIED): theory shows that a good pruning metric can turn power-law error scaling into exponential scaling in the size of the pruned dataset. Better-than-power-law scaling is observed for ResNets on CIFAR-10, SVHN and ImageNet. Most existing metrics scale poorly to ImageNet, and the best ones are costly and need labels. The new self-supervised prototype metric (k-means in an SSL embedding, distance to the nearest centroid) matches the best supervised metrics. A secondary source claims about 20% of ImageNet can be pruned without loss (UNVERIFIED).
items.relevance: Exponential scaling, if realized, is exactly the regime where compression sets become logarithmically small and sample-compression descriptions become short. In practice the prunable fraction at ImageNet scale is modest (about 20%), so the empirical evidence does not support k << m for hard tasks.

Counts come from one full training run, and examples are sorted by count. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS (UNVERIFIED): removing the least-forgotten examples lets up to 30% of CIFAR-10 be removed with comparable generalization, and up to 35% with less than a 0.2% rise in test error. items.relevance: A cheap, single-run selection statistic. Again, accuracy-preserving subsets are 65-70% of the data, orders of magnitude too large for a useful sample-compression bound. Forgetting counts do identify the hard examples a compression set must contain.

items.citation: Vitaly Feldman, Chiyuan Zhang. "What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation." NeurIPS 2020; arXiv:2008.03703. The arXiv page is blocked. I opened the official google-research code README.
items.finding: OPENED (README): confirms the authors, title and NeurIPS 2020. The authors release checkpoints of many models, each trained on the training set minus a random held-out subset: Inception on CIFAR-10 (239 GB) and CIFAR-100 (244 GB), ResNet50 on ImageNet (367 GB). These are used to estimate memorization, influence and consistency scores. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS (UNVERIFIED): subsampled estimates of influence and memorization are much cheaper than leave-one-out estimates. High-memorization examples are atypical, ambiguous or mislabeled. Removing memorized examples lowers test accuracy more than removing the same number of random examples. I did not retrieve exact accuracy drops or the subsample fraction.
items.relevance: A direct measurement of how predictions change when a network is retrained on a random subset. The long-tail training points flip, and their nearby test points flip with them. Any subset whose retrained g should agree with f on test inputs must contain these memorized examples, which bounds how small k can be for hard datasets.

items.citation: Baharan Mirzasoleiman, Jeff Bilmes, Jure Leskovec. "Coresets for Data-efficient Training of Machine Learning Models" (CRAIG). ICML 2020 (PMLR 119:6950-6960); arXiv:1906.01827. items.finding: UNVERIFIED (search snippets): selects a WEIGHTED subset whose weighted gradient approximates the full gradient. It does this by greedily maximizing a submodular facility-location function, which minimizes an upper bound on the gradient error. For convex problems, incremental gradient methods on the coreset converge to a near-optimal solution at the full-data rate, giving a |V|/|S| per-epoch speedup. Reported speedups: up to 6x for logistic regression and 3x for deep networks, with practically the same solution.

As a description of g, the weights must also be encoded, adding bits beyond the indices. Its gradient-matching objective could be pointed at f's own training trajectory to choose a subset that reproduces f.

items.citation: Andrew Ilyas, Sung Min Park, Logan Engstrom, Guillaume Leclerc, Aleksander Madry. "Datamodels: Predicting Predictions from Training Data." ICML 2022 (PMLR v162, published as "Datamodels: Understanding Predictions with Data and Data with Predictions"); arXiv:2202.00622. The arXiv page is blocked. I opened the official data-release README.
items.finding: OPENED (README): confirms the authors and title. For CIFAR-10 the authors trained 1,500,000 models on random 10% subsets, 750,000 on 20%, 300,000 on 50% and 600,000 on 75%, each plus 10,000 for evaluation. FMoW has 375k, 150k and 300k models at the 20/50/75% settings. They release train masks and per-example margins and logits for every model, and fit datamodels per target example with LASSO. FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS of the abstract (UNVERIFIED): simple linear datamodels, functions of which training examples are in the subset, predict the outputs of networks trained on subsets well. For 50% of CIFAR-10 test images, the prediction can be made incorrect by removing fewer than 200 target-specific training points (4% of the training set).
items.relevance: The most direct evidence on whether a network trained on a subset agrees with the full-data network. Each test point's output is close to a linear function of subset membership, so the expected agreement of g = A(S') with f can be predicted and optimized. Predictions are also brittle: small targeted removals flip them, so a random small subset will not reproduce f pointwise. The catch for the COMPUTE question: fitting datamodels took 10^5 to 10^6 trainings.

items.citation: Yiding Jiang, Vaishnavh Nagarajan, Christina Baek, J. Zico Kolter. "Assessing Generalization of SGD via Disagreement." ICLR 2022 (spotlight); arXiv:2106.13799. Related: Preetum Nakkiran, Yamini Bansal, "Distributional Generalization: A New Kind of Generalization", arXiv:2009.08092 (2020). BOTH UNVERIFIED: could not be opened.
items.finding: UNVERIFIED (search snippets of the abstract and slides): train the same architecture on the SAME training set with two SGD runs. Their disagreement rate on unlabeled test data approximately equals the test error. This is explained by class-wise calibration of the ensemble of SGD-trained models (the 'Generalization Disagreement Equality'). It is a stronger version of Nakkiran and Bansal's observation for interpolating classifiers, which needed independent training sets: there, test accuracy is about the agreement between two such classifiers.
items.relevance: The key quantitative fact for retraining-based surrogates. Two independently retrained networks disagree at a rate of about err(f). A surrogate g obtained by retraining on all the data or a subset, without fitting g to f, therefore has Pr[f != g] of about err(f) or more. The bound err(f) <= B(g) + Pr[f != g] then gives at best about 2*err(f) plus the compression term. Making Pr[f != g] << err(f) requires fitting g to f's outputs (distillation), not to the labels.

items.citation: Srinadh Bhojanapalli, Kimberly Wilber, Andreas Veit, Ankit Singh Rawat, Seungyeon Kim, Aditya Menon, Sanjiv Kumar (Google Research). "On the Reproducibility of Neural Network Predictions." arXiv:2102.03349, 2021. The co-author list beyond Bhojanapalli is from my memory, and I did not confirm a formal venue. items.finding: UNVERIFIED (search snippets): churn is the fraction of test examples on which two independently trained models disagree. It is substantial for ResNets on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet (Table 2; I did not retrieve the percentages). For example, five ResNet-v2-50 runs at about 76% top-1 on ImageNet differ markedly in their individual predictions. Churn appears even on correctly classified examples and is higher on misclassified ones. It persists even with a fixed seed and data order, because of platform nondeterminism. The proposed remedies are minimum-entropy regularizers and a co-distillation variant. Related, also UNVERIFIED: Summers and Dinneen (ICML 2021, PMLR 139:9913-9922) find that a one-bit change to the initial parameters produces run-to-run variability comparable to all other sources of nondeterminism.
items.relevance: Confirms that the run-to-run disagreement floor is large and hard to remove. A retraining-based g pays roughly this churn in the Pr[f != g] term even when its subset is perfect.

items.citation: Heinrich Jiang, Harikrishna Narasimhan, Dara Bahri, Andrew Cotter, Afshin Rostamizadeh. "Churn Reduction via Distillation." ICLR 2022; arXiv:2106.02654. UNVERIFIED: could not be opened.
items.finding: UNVERIFIED (search snippets): training with distillation, using the base model as the teacher, is equivalent to training under an explicit constraint on predictive churn relative to that base model. Experiments show distillation is strong for low-churn training against recent baselines, across fully-connected networks, convolutional networks and transformers. Bhojanapalli et al.'s entropy regularizers and co-distillation were found not effective at reducing churn with respect to a base model.
items.relevance: Distillation, i.e. training g on f's soft outputs, is the established way to make a retrained g agree with f beyond the churn floor. The caveat for certification: if g is distilled from f, which depends on all of S, or from extra unlabeled data, g is no longer a sample-compression predictor of a subset of S. Its certificate must then come from another route: counting g's description, or the uniform bound used in Bound to Disagree's distillation case. The unlabeled points used to certify Pr[f != g] must be fresh.

report.synthesis:
NETWORK CAVEAT: arxiv.org, openreview.net, proceedings.neurips.cc, jmlr.org, servicenow.com and every other paper host failed to resolve or were refused by the session proxy. Only raw.githubusercontent.com was reachable. Where possible I therefore 'opened' the authors' official code or data README on raw GitHub, and those items are marked verified=true: the opened page confirms authors, title and venue, and sometimes a key fact. All numbers marked 'FROM SEARCH SNIPPETS' come from search-engine extracts of arXiv abstracts and HTML and should be re-checked once arxiv.org is allowed in the session's network settings. Items with verified=false could not be opened at all.

MAIN TAKEAWAYS FOR THE COMPUTE QUESTION:

(1) The project's decomposition is already published. Bazinet, Zantedeschi and Germain, 'Bound to Disagree' (UAI 2026, arXiv:2602.23128), bound the risk of an untouched target network by a certified surrogate's bound plus a disagreement bound estimated on unlabeled data. The surrogates come from P2L sample compression, coresets (DeepCore), PACTL model compression, PAC-Bayes, quantization and distillation. This must be cited and benchmarked against. They report that the tightest bounds came without minimizing disagreement, which suggests the surrogate's own certificate is the bottleneck.

(2) Sample compression gives polynomial-compute search over a restricted, learner-defined program space: g = A(subset), costing about k*log2(e*m/k) bits plus a message. P2L (Paccagnan, Campi, Garatti, NeurIPS 2023; Campi and Garatti, JMLR 2023) finds the subset with k greedy retrainings instead of exponential enumeration. It works for CNNs on easy binary MNIST tasks, with compression sets of about 100 out of about 10^4 points, roughly 760 bits (Bazinet et al., AISTATS 2025). For CIFAR-10 (m = 50,000), a compression term k ln(e*m/k)/(m - k) of at most 0.1 needs k of about 1,000 (2%).

(3) The data-pruning literature says accuracy-preserving subsets are far larger than that. CIFAR-10 needs about 50% of the data (Paul et al. 2021, EL2N) or 65-70% (Toneva et al. 2019, forgetting). ImageNet allows only about 20% pruning (Sorscher et al. 2022, secondary figure). Score-based pruning provably fails at high compression, keeping 30% or less, where random selection is competitive (Ayed and Hayou, TMLR 2023). CRAIG-style gradient-matching coresets are polynomial with guarantees only in the convex case, and their weights add description bits. Sorscher et al.'s exponential-scaling theory is the regime where k would be small enough, but it is not realized on hard tasks.

(4) Agreement after retraining is limited by churn. Two SGD runs on the same data disagree at about the test error (Jiang, Nagarajan, Baek, Kolter, ICLR 2022; Nakkiran and Bansal 2020). Churn is substantial even with fixed seeds (Bhojanapalli et al. 2021), and a one-bit change to the initialization matters as much as all other sources of nondeterminism (Summers and Dinneen, ICML 2021, UNVERIFIED). So a subset-retrained g typically has Pr[f != g] of about err(f) or more, and the bound is at best about 2*err(f) plus the compression term. Datamodels (Ilyas et al., ICML 2022) show that subset-trained outputs are nearly linear in subset membership, which makes agreement predictable. They also show brittleness: removing fewer than 200 targeted points (4%) flips 50% of CIFAR-10 test predictions, and fitting the datamodels took more than 10^6 trainings. Feldman and Zhang (NeurIPS 2020) show that the long-tail, memorized examples must be in any subset that reproduces f.

(5) Distillation is how to get Pr[f != g] << err(f) (Jiang et al., 'Churn Reduction via Distillation', ICLR 2022). But a g distilled from f, or fitted on extra data, is no longer a sample-compression predictor of S. Its certificate must then come from description-length counting or a uniform bound, and the disagreement must be certified on fresh D_X samples.

(6) Worst-case sample-compression theory is uninformative for neural networks. Moran and Yehudayoff give a scheme size of exp(O(d)), and the O(d) conjecture of Littlestone and Warmuth (1986) and Floyd and Warmuth (1995) is still open.

NET: subsampling the TRAINING DATA yields efficiently searchable short surrogates only on easy tasks. On harder tasks, both the subset size and the retraining churn make it weaker than distillation-plus-compression of f itself.

ADDITIONAL LEADS, all UNVERIFIED and not opened:
- Nguyen, Novak, Xiao, Lee, NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2107.13034), KIP dataset distillation: 10 synthetic images (0.02% of the data) reach over 64-65% CIFAR-10 accuracy. These are not training points, so this is not sample compression, and continuous pixels cost many bits.
- Comeau et al. 2025, 'Sample Compression for Self-Certified Continual Learning' (arXiv:2503.10503).
- Balachandran 2026, 'Pay Only for Disagreement' (arXiv:2609.17560): certifies model updates via disagreement on unlabeled traffic.

Existence, authors, venue and year are CONFIRMED from the published PDF (PMLR 337, pp. 491-520, OpenReview CZeG5HW1Y5). Corrections and details from the full text:
(1) Theorem numbering. The zero-one disagreement bound is THEOREM 5 in the UAI version: R_D(f) <= R_D(h) + Bin(m*d_U(f,h), m, delta), an inverted binomial tail of the empirical disagreement on an unlabeled set U of size m. Theorem 4 is McAllester's PAC-Bayes bound. Theorem 6 covers Lipschitz losses. Theorem 7 covers non-Lipschitz losses and needs a LABELED held-out set.
(2) Independence. U is a 'disagreement set' carved out before training: 20% of the training data for MNIST and CIFAR10, 85% for Amazon polarity. Theorem 5 holds with probability over U for fixed f and h, so U must be independent of both.
(3) Surrogates. The README lists five scripts: P2L, coresets, model compression (PACTL/SubLoRA), PAC-Bayes (PBB) and quantization. Distillation appears only in a hardware note. The paper has three certified-surrogate frameworks (sample compression, model compression, PAC-Bayes). Distillation is 'use case #2': it uses Eq. 4, a union bound over all h, so h may be trained on S and U with pseudo-labels from f. Quantization is 'use case #3': it bounds the risk gap only, because the quantized models are too large for non-vacuous bounds. The coreset methods tested are Random Coreset, k-Center Greedy, Forgetting and DeepFool. The paper argues that 'a coreset can be viewed as the compression set' (confirmed).
(4) Numbers, zero-one bounds on the TARGET network (Table 2, %). Target test error is 0.50 on MNIST (CNN) and 5.84 on CIFAR10 (ResNet18).

Existence, authors, NeurIPS 2023 and spotlight status are confirmed by several listings. The abstract copy confirms the main claim: any learning algorithm is embedded in a meta-algorithm (P2L) to instill compression properties. On MNIST classification and a synthetic regression problem, P2L 'attains generalization bounds that compare favorably with the state of the art (test-set and PAC-Bayes bounds)' and 'learns models with better post-training performance'.
One precision on the algorithm, as given in Algorithm 1 of Bazinet et al. 2025. P2L starts from an initial predictor h0 (random or pretrained), not from training on an empty set. It adds the point with the largest loss, retrains A on the compression set, and repeats until the model makes zero errors on the complement. The P2L bound (Paccagnan et al. Theorem 4.2) holds only in this consistent case. Batch (R = 32) and early-stopping variants exist (Marks and Paccagnan 2025).
Caveat for the project's relevance note. Relabeling S with f's labels breaks the i.i.d. sample that the compression bound assumes, because f depends on S. Certify Pr[f != g] on fresh unlabeled data instead.

items.citation: Mingjie Sun, Zhuang Liu, Anna Bair, J. Zico Kolter. 'A Simple and Effective Pruning Approach for Large Language Models' (Wanda: Pruning by Weights and Activations). arXiv:2306.11695, 2023. The ICLR 2024 venue is from memory; the README lists only arXiv.
items.finding: From the README (opened): each weight W_ij is scored by |W_ij| times ||X_j||_2, the weight's magnitude times the norm of its input activation on a small calibration set. Weights are removed per output row. The core method has no retraining and no weight update; OBS-style updates appear only as an ablation. WikiText perplexity on LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B at 50% unstructured sparsity is 6.42/5.56/3.98, against dense 5.12/4.57/3.12. At 2:4 sparsity it is 11.02/8.27/5.16; SparseGPT does better at 7B (10.17). Plain magnitude pruning at 2:4 on 7B gives 54.59. UNVERIFIED (memory): pruning takes seconds to minutes, far faster than SparseGPT.
items.relevance: The Wanda score is the per-weight version of the project's Maurey importance s_i = ||a_i|| * ||phi_i||_{L2(D_X)}: a weight times the L2(D_X) norm of the signal it multiplies. Large-scale evidence: this statistic costs a few forward passes and finds a subnetwork with almost unchanged outputs, while magnitude alone, without the activation-norm factor, collapses. That supports sampling or top-k selection by s_i at the weight level as well as the unit level. Caveat: 50% sparsity shows high fidelity, not a short description; L(g) barely shrinks.

LLaMA Wiki2 perplexity, in the order FP16 / 4-bit GPTQ / 3-bit GPTQ / 3-bit with group size 128: 7B 5.68 / 6.09 / 8.07 / 6.61; 65B 3.53 / 3.84 / 5.04 / 4.17. UNVERIFIED (memory): all three solve, layer by layer, min over W' of ||WX - W'X||_F^2 on calibration inputs X, with greedy second-order (OBS) updates using H = XX^T. The SparseGPT abstract says OPT-175B and BLOOM-176B are pruned in under 4.5 hours to 50-60% sparsity with negligible perplexity increase. The GPTQ abstract says a 175B model is quantized to 3-4 bits in about 4 GPU hours.
items.relevance: The strongest practical evidence that finding a g close to f need not take exponential search. A layer-wise least-squares objective on samples from D_X, exactly the known-D_X setting, is solved greedily in polynomial time at 175B scale. GPTQ against round-to-nearest shows that error feedback is what makes 3-bit codes viable. The cost for an Occam bound: L(g) stays at about 3-4 bits per weight, far above m for any realistic training set unless combined with much stronger sparsity or entropy coding. Fidelity is measured by perplexity, not by Pr[f != g]; the project's sampling certificate would supply the missing guarantee.

items.citation: Jinjie Zhang, Yixuan Zhou, Rayan Saab. 'Post-training Quantization for Neural Networks with Provable Guarantees.' SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science 5(2):373-399, 2023. arXiv:2201.11113. Earlier work: Eric Lybrand, Rayan Saab, 'A Greedy Algorithm for Quantizing Neural Networks', JMLR 22, 2021 (UNVERIFIED, from memory).
items.finding: From the README (opened): GPFQ is a post-training quantizer built on a greedy path-following mechanism, and it has a sparse mode. For a single-layer network, 'the relative square error essentially decays linearly in the number of weights', so over-parameterization helps. It is applied to AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet at several bit widths (e.g. 4 bits). The page gives neither the exact bound nor accuracy numbers. UNVERIFIED (memory): each weight is rounded so that the accumulated error in the layer's pre-activations on the data stays small, a Sigma-Delta-style error feedback. The theorem assumes random (e.g. Gaussian) input data.
items.relevance: One of the few compression procedures with a theorem on the output deviation ||f - g||_{L2(data)} of a trained layer, as opposed to a random one. It is deterministic and polynomial-time, and its error improves with width. Maurey sampling behaves the other way: its error A^2/k grows as k shrinks. It fits the project's pipeline: GPFQ-quantize the (possibly subsampled) network, entropy-code it, then certify Pr[f != g] on fresh samples. This lowers the bits per weight in L(g) directly.

items.citation: Alireza Aghasi, Afshin Abdi, Nam Nguyen, Justin Romberg. 'Net-Trim: Convex Pruning of Deep Neural Networks with Performance Guarantee.' NIPS 2017, arXiv:1611.05162. The title is read from the README's NIPS link. Journal follow-up: arXiv:1806.06457, Aghasi, Abdi, Romberg, 'Fast Convex Pruning of Deep Neural Networks', SIAM J. Math. Data Sci. 2020 (title and venue from memory). Related: Xin Dong, Shangyu Chen, Sinno Jialin Pan, 'Learning to Prune Deep Neural Networks via Layer-wise Optimal Brain Surgeon', NIPS 2017, arXiv:1705.07565; its README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/csyhhu/L-OBS/HEAD/README.md) confirms the title and venue.
items.finding: From the READMEs (opened): Net-Trim solves a convex program per layer, in a regularized and a constrained form. L-OBS computes a per-layer Hessian inverse and prunes with it; for ResNet-50 that takes about 33 hours on a 64-CPU server. Neither README states a guarantee. UNVERIFIED (memory). Net-Trim replaces each layer by the l1-minimal weights whose ReLU outputs on the training inputs stay within eps of the original; with the activation pattern fixed this is a linear or convex program. The parallel scheme bounds the final-output discrepancy by a sum of the per-layer eps; in the cascade scheme the error grows with depth. For Gaussian-like inputs, about s*log(N/s) samples suffice to recover an s-sparse layer. L-OBS proves that the final-output error is at most a weighted sum of per-layer reconstruction errors.
items.relevance: These are the multi-layer analogue that the project's one-hidden-layer Maurey argument lacks. The search is efficient (convex or second-order), and there is an explicit bound on how per-layer output deviations propagate to the final output. The recipe fits the known-D_X setting: fit each layer on samples from D_X, then certify Pr[f != g] on fresh samples. The search can use the data freely without breaking validity, which is the project's Proposition 1.

items.citation: Francis Bach. 'On the Equivalence between Kernel Quadrature Rules and Random Feature Expansions.' JMLR 18(21):1-38, 2017. arXiv:1502.06800. Related: Alessandro Rudi, Lorenzo Rosasco, 'Generalization Properties of Learning with Random Features', NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1602.04474; Ahmed El Alaoui, Michael W. Mahoney, 'Fast Randomized Kernel Methods with Statistical Guarantees', NeurIPS 2015 (ridge leverage scores for Nystrom). UNVERIFIED: nothing was opened; arxiv.org does not resolve in this session.
items.finding: UNVERIFIED (memory). The setting is approximating a function by k sampled features (units) and then refitting the output weights by ridge regression with parameter lambda. Sampling units from the optimized distribution q(v), proportional to the ridge leverage score <phi_v, (Sigma + lambda I)^{-1} phi_v>, makes k = O(d(lambda) log(d(lambda)/delta)) enough for squared L2 error O(lambda). Here d(lambda) = tr Sigma(Sigma + lambda I)^{-1} is the degrees of freedom. Sampling from the base or norm distribution instead needs k of order (max leverage)/lambda, up to about 1/lambda, which is Maurey-like. For eigenvalue decay mu_j ~ j^{-alpha}, d(lambda) ~ lambda^{-1/alpha}. Rudi and Rosasco: O(sqrt(n) log n) random features reach the optimal kernel ridge rate, and leverage-score sampling needs fewer.
items.relevance: This would sharpen the project's Proposition 4 for its 'top-k with refit' variant. Treat the N trained units as columns: the units' feature map phi_i under D_X. Ridge-leverage sampling plus a least-squares refit then replaces A^2/(k*gamma^2) with a bound set by the effective dimension of the units' covariance under D_X, which can be far smaller than the path-norm bound. The leverage scores come from the N x N Gram matrix of the phi_i on samples from D_X, so they cost polynomial time. This is the standard optimal importance-sampling answer for subsample-then-refit; Maurey or Barron norm sampling is the no-refit special case.

Related: Grant Rotskoff, Eric Vanden-Eijnden, 'Trainability and Accuracy of Artificial Neural Networks: An Interacting Particle System Approach', CPAM 2022, arXiv:1805.00915; Justin Sirignano, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, 'Mean Field Analysis of Neural Networks: A Law of Large Numbers', SIAM J. items.finding: UNVERIFIED (memory). For f(x) = (1/N) sum_i sigma(x; theta_i), SGD with step size eps tracks a PDE for the distribution of the neurons rho_t (the 'distributional dynamics'). Up to time T, the risk of the N-unit SGD network is within K e^{KT} * sqrt(max(1/N, eps)) * (sqrt(D + log(N/eps)) + z) of the limit risk R(rho_t), with probability 1 - e^{-z^2}. Neurons behave approximately as i.i.d. draws from rho_t (propagation of chaos). Rotskoff and Vanden-Eijnden give law-of-large-numbers and fluctuation results, with loss fluctuations of order 1/N around the limit.
items.relevance: This is the theory that predicts when uniform neuron subsampling of a trained network works. In mean-field scaling the N trained units are roughly an i.i.d. sample from rho_t. A uniform random subset of k units, rescaled by N/k, is then roughly a k-unit SGD solution, with a risk gap of about sqrt(D/k) up to logs and a width-independent k. That matches the project's mean-field bullet, where A = O(1). Limits: the e^{KT} constant makes it non-quantitative, and NTK-scaled networks are outside it. It complements Chen et al. (dynamical CLT) and Shevchenko-Mondelli (dropout stability), which are already on the list.

items.citation: Emmanuel Abbe, Samy Bengio, Aryo Lotfi, Kevin Rizk. 'Generalization on the Unseen, Logic Reasoning and Degree Curriculum.' ICML 2023, PMLR 202:31-60. arXiv:2301.13105.
items.finding: From the README (opened): title, authors, ICML 2023, PMLR 202 pp. 31-60, and that the tasks are defined in examples.py with hyperparameters in script.sh. UNVERIFIED (memory). The tasks are Boolean functions on {+-1}^n where part of the domain (e.g. x_1 = 1) never appears in training. Networks trained by (S)GD (random-feature models, diagonal linear networks, MLPs, Transformers) tend to output the 'min-degree interpolator': the interpolant of the training data with the least Fourier-Walsh mass at high degree, i.e. a lexicographically minimal degree profile. This is proved for random features with small steps and for diagonal linear networks, and shown experimentally for MLPs and Transformers. The paper also proposes a Degree-Curriculum algorithm.
items.relevance: Evidence specific to Boolean inputs that trained networks sit near low-degree functions even off the training support, so the Walsh spectrum of f concentrates on low degrees. That is exactly the condition under which a polynomial-time structured search finds a short g. One option is the Linial-Mansour-Nisan low-degree algorithm (estimate every degree-<=d Walsh coefficient of f by sampling, about n^d poly(1/eps) evaluations of f). The other is Kushilevitz-Mansour with queries. Both can be run on f directly, since samples from D_X are unlimited.

items.finding: From the code (opened; the README at .../HEAD/README.md was also opened): a 1-layer transformer with d_model = 128 is trained on addition mod p = 113, using 30% of the pairs for training (frac_train = 0.3) and weight decay 1.0. Key frequencies are computed from the neuron activations (calculate_key_freqs), not hard-coded. The 'restricted loss' (calculate_trig_loss) recomputes the loss from the logit components at the key frequencies only, and an 'excluded loss' ablates them. UNVERIFIED (memory): the grokked network implements a discrete-Fourier / trig-identity algorithm with about 5 key frequencies, and the restricted loss is lower than the full loss, so projecting f onto the short algorithm improves it.
items.relevance: A concrete case where a trained f is eps-close to a program of a few dozen bits: about 5 frequencies out of 56, roughly 5*log2(56), about 29 bits, plus the fixed algorithm. The surrogate is found by a polynomial white-box structured search, a DFT of the embeddings, not by enumeration. It illustrates the project's Proposition 2 (simple target implies closeness) and is the underlying case study for Gross et al. 2024 (compact proofs), which the project already cites.

gaps.synthesis:
Search conditions. I could not run any web search: the turn's shared budget of 200 searches was already used up. arxiv.org and proceedings.mlr.press do not resolve here; they must be allowed in the session's network settings for arXiv or PMLR pages to be opened. The GitHub MCP tool is limited to kaarelh/ai-works. Following the tool's advice, I did not probe more hosts. I chose candidates from memory and from gaps in the project's literature.md and search/README.md, and verified them only through official code READMEs and source on raw.githubusercontent.com. Every claim not on those pages is marked UNVERIFIED (memory).

Main gaps in the existing list, in order of importance:

1. **Theory of subsampling with refit.** The list has Maurey/Barron sampling without refit. The standard improvement is ridge-leverage-score sampling (Bach, JMLR 2017; Rudi & Rosasco, NeurIPS 2017; El Alaoui & Mahoney, NeurIPS 2015). After a least-squares refit, the number of units needed scales with the effective dimension d(lambda) of the trained units' features under D_X, not with A^2/gamma^2. The scores are computable in polynomial time from samples of D_X. This is the natural next experiment after s_i-proportional sampling.

2. **Why uniform subsampling works for trained networks.** Mean-field propagation of chaos (Mei-Montanari-Nguyen, PNAS 2018; Rotskoff-Vanden-Eijnden; Sirignano-Spiliopoulos) says SGD-trained units are roughly i.i.d. from rho_t. So a random k-subset is roughly a k-unit SGD solution, with a width-independent k. The constants are non-quantitative, and NTK scaling falls outside the theory.

3. **Practical post-training compression.** OBC, GPTQ, SparseGPT, Wanda, GPFQ, Net-Trim and L-OBS solve layer-wise output-matching problems on samples from D_X in polynomial time, at scales up to 175B parameters. Examples: LLaMA-65B at 4-bit GPTQ has perplexity 3.84 against 3.53 dense; LLaMA-2-70B at 50% Wanda sparsity has 3.98 against 3.12. Wanda's score |W| * ||X|| is the weight-level form of the project's Maurey importance s_i. GPFQ and Net-Trim/L-OBS add provable output-error bounds and depth-propagation bounds. The catch for Occam bounds is that L(g) stays around 3-4 bits per weight or 50% density. They show the search for a high-fidelity g is easy; they do not show that a short g exists.

4. **Closeness to simple functions on Boolean inputs.** Abbe et al.'s min-degree bias (ICML 2023) suggests trained networks have concentrated low-degree Walsh spectra. That is the condition under which the Linial-Mansour-Nisan low-degree algorithm or Kushilevitz-Mansour finds a short g efficiently. Nanda et al. (ICLR 2023) is a worked case of a trained network close to a program of about 30 bits, found by a DFT rather than by search.

Further leads I could not open (all UNVERIFIED):
- Linial, Mansour, Nisan, 'Constant depth circuits, Fourier transform, and learnability', JACM 1993: the low-degree algorithm, a natural companion to the Kushilevitz-Mansour entry.
- Craven & Shavlik, 'Extracting Tree-Structured Representations of Trained Networks' (TREPAN), NIPS 1995: query-based extraction of a short tree surrogate, measured by fidelity.
- Carlini, Jagielski, Mironov, 'Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Network Models', CRYPTO 2020 (arXiv:2003.04884), and Jagielski et al., 'High Accuracy and High Fidelity Extraction of Neural Networks', USENIX Security 2020 (arXiv:1909.01838). Black-box queries recover real ReLU networks efficiently, which bears on how much the project's PRF-hardness Proposition 3 matters in practice. My guessed repo URL for Carlini et al. returned 404.
- Frankle & Carbin, 'The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis', ICLR 2019, and Frankle et al., 'Linear Mode Connectivity and the LTH' (arXiv:1912.05671). The open_lth README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/facebookresearch/open_lth/HEAD/README.md, opened) confirms these citations and the rewinding procedure, but no sparsity numbers.
- Yang & Salman, 'A Fine-Grained Spectral Perspective on Neural Networks' (arXiv:1907.10599). The NNspectra README (opened) confirms code for NTK and conjugate-kernel eigenvalues on the Boolean cube and a 'Clarifying Simplicity Bias' notebook; no claims were read.
